articles.title: Álvares Machado cancela Facam para investir em Samu e Bombeiros | G1
articles.standfirst: Comunicado divulgado nas redes sociais da prefeitura afirma que a tradicional festa custa R$ 2 milhões por três dias de evento. A Facam é realizada com recursos próprios do município.
articles.summary: A tradicional festa em celebração ao aniversário de Álvares Machado (SP) foi cancelada para este ano. A previsão era que a Facam ocorresse na última semana de novembro.
articles.body:
Prefeitura Municipal de Álvares Machado (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Google Maps

A tradicional Feira Agropecuária e Comercial de Álvares Machado , festa em celebração ao aniversário do município, foi cancelada para este ano. A previsão era de que o evento ocorresse na última semana de novembro, como nos anos anteriores.

O comunicado do cancelamento da Facam foi divulgado nas redes sociais da prefeitura na terça-feira (13). Segundo o conteúdo, os três dias de evento custam R$ 2 milhões ao município.

Ainda conforme o vídeo divulgado, a previsão é que parte desse valor seja investida em Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (SAMU) e Corpo de Bombeiros, com custo anual de R$ 1,1 milhão para o município.

Ao g1 , a Prefeitura de Álvares Machado (SP) informou que a Facam sempre foi realizada com recursos próprios da administração municipal.

Além disso, nos últimos dois anos, a prefeitura contou com parceria do Ministério do Turismo, por meio de recursos destinados exclusivamente ao pagamento dos shows. No entanto, as demais despesas do evento eram pagas com recursos municipais.

A prefeitura destacou que para a edição do ano passado o repasse do governo federal foi feito apenas em abril deste ano e, por isso, o município precisou arcar integralmente com os pagamentos dos shows, utilizando recursos próprios.

Em 2025 ocorreu a 26ª edição do evento, que recebeu shows das duplas Thaeme e Thiago e Matheus & Kauan.

Como não foi possível utilizar a verba do governo federal para o pagamento dos shows, pois eles já haviam sido pagos, o dinheiro permaneceu nos cofres públicos, aguardando o posicionamento do Ministério do Turismo para fazer a devolução.

Conforme a prefeitura, para a edição deste ano, a verba federal não havia sido recebida. O evento estava começando a ser organizado quando a administração decidiu cancelar a edição.

Em nota, o Ministério do Turismo informou ao g1 que o repasse financeiro do convênio com Álvares Machado, firmado em 26 de novembro de 2025, no valor de R$ 250 mil, ocorreu em 16 de abril de 2026.

Como a Prefeitura de Álvares Machado optou por pagar os cachês dos shows com recursos próprios – e solicitou o reembolso –, o recurso ficou “paralisado” em uma conta específica, segundo o governo federal, destinada exclusivamente para transferência do dinheiro do convênio.

O Ministério do Turismo acrescentou que já concluiu a análise do pedido de reembolso e, por exigência legal, aguarda o fim do período de defeso eleitoral para autorizar a transferência do recurso desta conta específica para o município.

A pasta informou que seguia à disposição da prefeitura para prestar as orientações necessárias.

Conforme a Prefeitura de Álvares Machado, o cancelamento da Facam 2026 ocorreu para priorizar os investimentos necessários à construção da base do Corpo de Bombeiros no município e implantação do Samu.

Para realizar essas iniciativas, a prefeitura disse na quarta-feira (14) que já assinou o convênio com o Governo do Estado e está dando andamento às tratativas e aos procedimentos necessários para a implantação da unidade.

“A previsão é abrir o processo licitatório para a construção da base, com expectativa de instalação e inauguração em março de 2027, durante as comemorações do padroeiro do município.”

Segundo a prefeitura, o cronograma poderá sofrer alterações em função de fatores como as condições climáticas e o andamento das obras.

Já no caso do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu), o município disse que estava finalizando os procedimentos relacionados ao convênio com o Governo Federal.

Para o Samu, também estava prevista a realização de concurso para a contratação dos profissionais que atuarão no serviço, segundo a prefeitura.

articles.title: Lula defende pela primeira vez redução da maioridade penal para crimes hediondos | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente afirmou em entrevista à TV Globo ser favorável à mudança, mas disse que o tema deve ser discutido separadamente da PEC da Segurança. Proposta semelhante apresentada pelo líder do PT no Senado dividiu governistas.
articles.summary: Presidente afirmou em entrevista à TV Globo ser favorável à mudança, mas disse que o tema deve ser discutido separadamente da PEC da Segurança. Proposta semelhante apresentada pelo líder do PT no Senado dividiu governistas.
articles.body:
A manifestação de Lula ocorreu depois de a propostad dato à reeleição, afirmou em entrevista à TV Globo ser favorável à redução da maioridade penal de 18 para 16 anos nos casos de crimes hediondos.

Essa foi a primeira vez que ele falou sobre o tema de forma contundente, ao responder uma pergunta da jornalista Renata Lo Prete nesta quinta-feira (15) ( leia mais abaixo ).

Mais cedo, uma proposta semelhante provocou divergências entre integrantes do governo e do PT no Senado.

A ideia defendida pelo presidente é reduzir para 16 anos a idade a partir da qual adolescentes que cometerem crimes hediondos podem responder criminalmente como adultos.

Entre esses crimes estão homicídio qualificado, latrocínio, extorsão mediante sequestro e estupro.

"O meu pensamento, enquanto cidadão brasileiro, todo e qualquer crime hediondo, eu sou favorável a diminuir a pena. Para crimes hediondos. Eu sou a favor, sou a favor", afirmou Lula.

Lula não costuma tratar da redução da maioridade penal em seus discursos públicos. A entrevista desta quinta foi a primeira vez nesta campanha em que o petista explicitou uma posição sobre o tema.

Até então, ao falar de segurança pública, Lula vinha concentrando seu discurso no combate ao crime organizado e na defesa da PEC da Segurança.

Na sequência, Lo Prete perguntou diretamente se o presidente defendia reduzir a maioridade penal. Lula respondeu que sim e, questionado especificamente sobre a idade de 16 anos, voltou a manifestar apoio à medida.

O presidente ressalvou, no entanto, que a mudança não deveria ser incluída na PEC da Segurança Pública que está em análise no Congresso.

"Primeiro você discute a PEC, aprova a PEC e aí você pode discutir a maioridade penal ou não", disse.

Senado adia votação da PEC da Segurança Pública por falta de acordo no governo sobre a redução da maioridade penal — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A manifestação de Lula ocorreu depois de a proposta de redução da maioridade penal provocar um impasse entre governistas no Senado.

Nesta quinta, Camilo Santana, líder do PT no Senado, apresentou uma emenda à PEC da Segurança para reduzir a maioridade penal para 16 anos nos casos de crimes hediondos.

A iniciativa representou mudança em relação à posição historicamente adotada por governistas no Congresso, contrária à redução.

A proposta de Camilo foi apresentada em reação a uma ofensiva da oposição. O senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) apresentou uma emenda que reduz a maioridade para 16 anos na maior parte dos crimes e para 14 anos em uma relação de crimes graves.

Parte do PT, porém, se posicionou contra a inclusão da mudança na PEC da Segurança. Integrantes do partido defenderam que uma alteração dessa dimensão fosse discutida com mais calma.

Sem acordo sobre as emendas, o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), retirou a PEC da Segurança da pauta nesta quinta-feira.

A posição manifestada por Lula também coincidiu com o argumento de que a maioridade penal deve ser discutida separadamente da PEC da Segurança. Mais cedo, o ex-ministro e coordenador da campanha de reeleição do presidente Rui Costa havia afirmado que o governo defendia deixar o debate sobre a redução da maioridade para outro momento.

Atualmente, a Constituição estabelece a maioridade penal aos 18 anos. Há também uma proposta específica em tramitação no Congresso para reduzir essa idade.

Em junho, a Comissão de Constituição e Justiça da Câmara aprovou, por 44 votos a 18, uma PEC que estabelece a maioridade penal aos 16 anos.

O texto ainda precisa passar por comissão especial e pelo plenário da Câmara antes de uma eventual análise do Senado.

articles.title: Moraes autoriza Augusto Heleno a deixar prisão domiciliar para consulta médica em Brasília | G1
articles.standfirst: General deverá ir ao Hospital das Forças Armadas em 22 de outubro para retorno ambulatorial de neurocirurgia. Ministro também permitiu internação urgente, caso haja indicação médica, sem necessidade de autorização judicial prévia.
articles.summary: General deverá ir ao Hospital das Forças Armadas em 22 de outubro para retorno ambulatorial de neurocirurgia. Ministro também permitiu internação urgente, caso haja indicação médica, sem necessidade de autorização judicial prévia.
articles.body:
O ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), autorizou o general da reserva Augusto Heleno Ribeiro Pereira a deixar a prisão domiciliar no dia 22 de outubro para uma consulta médica no Hospital das Forças Armadas (HFA), em Brasília.

Segundo a decisão, Heleno poderá se deslocar às 10h para um retorno ambulatorial de neurocirurgia. A autorização vale apenas pelo período necessário para a ida ao hospital e o retorno.

Após o atendimento, a defesa terá 24 horas para apresentar ao STF um documento que comprove a realização do procedimento.

Moraes também autorizou que Heleno seja internado com urgência, sem necessidade de uma nova decisão judicial, caso haja orientação médica. Heleno faz acompanhamento para um quadro de demência ( leia mais abaixo ).

Na hipótese de internação, o STF deverá ser informado em até 24 horas, com a comprovação da necessidade da internação.

A autorização é provisória e não altera as demais medidas cautelares impostas ao general, conforme a decisão.

Heleno cumpre prisão domiciliar humanitária desde dezembro de 2025 e usa tornozeleira eletrônica. O ex-ministro do Gabinete de Segurança Institucional (GSI) no governo de Jair Bolsonaro foi condenado a 21 anos de prisão no processo da trama golpista.

A prisão domiciliar foi concedida por Moraes após perícia médica e em razão do quadro de saúde do general.

Na ocasião, a decisão que concedeu a prisão domiciliar estabeleceu que Heleno deveria pedir autorização para deslocamentos por questões de saúde.

Para situações de urgência ou emergência, havia exceção, com necessidade de justificativa posterior.

Augusto Heleno durante interrogatório na Primeira Turma do STF — Foto: Foto: Ton Molina/STF

Em uma decisão anterior, de 13 de outubro, Moraes já havia autorizado visitas médicas diárias a Heleno. O pedido havia sido feito pelo Comando Militar do Planalto.

Segundo o documento, o acompanhamento foi solicitado por causa do quadro clínico do general, descrito como diagnóstico de “demência de origem mista, de natureza progressiva e irreversível”.

Moraes autorizou que duas médicas militares realizassem as visitas diariamente. A mesma decisão registra que Heleno tinha 79 anos, cumpria prisão domiciliar humanitária desde 22 de dezembro de 2025 e havia cumprido 308 dias de pena até 13 de outubro de 2026.

articles.title: Congresso promulga fim da escala 6x1 em primeira mudança da jornada de trabalho desde 1988 e garante dois dias de folga por semana | G1
articles.standfirst: Jornada máxima será reduzida gradualmente de 44 para 40 horas semanais, sem redução salarial; mudança começa a produzir efeitos após período de transição.
articles.summary: Jornada máxima será reduzida gradualmente de 44 para 40 horas semanais, sem redução salarial; mudança começa a produzir efeitos após período de transição.
articles.body:
O Congresso Nacional promulgou nesta sexta-feira (16) a emenda à Constituição que acaba com a escala de trabalho 6x1 e garante aos trabalhadores dois dias de repouso remunerado por semana, sem redução salarial. É a primeira mudança na jornada de trabalho em 38 anos, desde a Constituição de 1988.

Durante a Constituinte a redução de 48 horas semanais para 40 horas foi discutida. Mas sem apoio suficiente, a jornada ficou em 44 horas. Agora, a Constituição passa a prever o limite máximo de 40 horas, com duas folgas por semana em todo o país.

A mudança reduz gradualmente a jornada máxima de trabalho de 44 para 40 horas semanais . A sessão solene de promulgação ocorreu no plenário do Senado. O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), e o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), participaram da cerimônia.

As novas regras, no entanto, não têm efeito imediato. A emenda ainda precisa ser publicada no Diário Oficial, o que pode ocorrer ainda nesta sexta ( leia mais abaixo ).

Antes da abertura oficial da sessão, o presidente do Senado “quebrou o protocolo” e pediu uma cadeira para o senador Paulo Paim (PT-RS) na Mesa.

Paim participou da Assembleia Nacional Constituinte de 1988, quando era deputado federal e atuou nas negociações que reduziram a jornada de trabalho de 48 para 44 horas semanais. O parlamentar também participou das discussões sobre o fim da escala 6x1 no Senado.

A partir da publicação, começa a contar o prazo de dois meses para a primeira etapa da transição , quando a jornada máxima passa de 44 para 42 horas semanais e os trabalhadores passam a ter direito aos dois dias de repouso remunerado.

A emenda altera o artigo 7º da Constituição, que trata dos direitos dos trabalhadores. Um dos dois dias de descanso deverá ser, preferencialmente, aos domingos.

Na prática, a garantia de dois dias de repouso impede a adoção regular da chamada escala 6x1, na qual o trabalhador atua seis dias e folga um.

Por se tratar de uma mudança na Constituição, o texto não depende de sanção presidencial. A promulgação é feita pelo Congresso.

Congresso marca a promulgação do fim da escala 6x1 para sexta-feira (16) — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

dois meses após a promulgação: a jornada máxima cai de 44 para 42 horas semanais, com dois dias de repouso remunerado;

12 meses depois da primeira redução: o limite passa definitivamente a 40 horas semanais, sem redução salarial.

A mudança também pode afetar trabalhadores que já cumprem jornada de segunda a sexta-feira e atualmente compensam durante a semana as horas que seriam trabalhadas no sábado.

As duas folgas não precisam necessariamente ocorrer sábado e domingo, porque a distribuição pode variar conforme a escala.

A redução da jornada não elimina horas extras nem mecanismos como o banco de horas.

O Senado aprovou a proposta na quarta-feira (14), em dois turnos. Foram 75 votos favoráveis e um contrário nas duas votações. Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS) foi o único senador a votar contra o texto.

A aprovação ocorreu a 11 dias do segundo turno da eleição presidencial e representou uma vitória política para Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, que transformou o fim da escala 6x1 em uma das bandeiras de sua campanha à reeleição.

Após a votação, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva classificou a aprovação como uma "vitória dos trabalhadores e trabalhadoras".

Aposentadoria especial para agentes de saúde

Na mesma sessão, o Congresso também promulgou a emenda que estabelece aposentadoria especial para agentes comunitários de saúde e agentes de combate às endemias.

A proposta havia sido aprovada pelo Senado em julho, por 73 votos a 1, nos dois turnos, além de uma abstenção.

O texto estabelece idade mínima de 57 anos para mulheres e 60 anos para homens, desde que cumpridos 25 anos de contribuição e de exercício na atividade. Também prevê aposentadoria integral com paridade para os servidores alcançados pelas regras.

À época da aprovação, a medida era considerada uma "pauta-bomba" pelo governo. Uma projeção do Ministério da Previdência apontava impacto fiscal de R$ 27 bilhões em dez anos.

articles.title: Falta de água em Petrolina: veja lista de 60 bairros afetados | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Compesa, houve um problema imprevisto na retomada do sistema na noite de quinta-feira (15). Previsão é que o serviço seja restabelecido gradativamente a partir das 13h desta sexta (16).
articles.summary: A falta de água em Petrolina atinge 60 localidades após falha na manutenção da Compesa; serviço deve ser normalizado gradualmente a partir desta sexta-feira (16).
articles.body:
Torneira sem água. — Foto: Pedro França/Agência Senado

A Companhia Pernambucana de Saneamento (Compesa) realiza, nesta sexta-feira (16), um trabalho emergencial para restabelecer o abastecimento de água em Petrolina , no Sertão de Pernambuco. Uma parada programada, que deveria ter sido concluída na quinta-feira (15), precisou ser estendida após um problema técnico na retomada do sistema.

A suspensão temporária do abastecimento começou na quarta-feira (14) para serviços de manutenção corretiva e melhorias nas Estações de Tratamento de Água (ETAs) do município.

Segundo a Compesa, ao iniciar a retomada da distribuição a partir da ETA Centro, na noite de quinta, houve uma "ocorrência" técnica — a companhia não detalhou a gravidade do problema. Equipes trabalham no local e a previsão é que os reparos sejam concluídos até as 13h desta sexta-feira (16), quando o abastecimento será retomado de forma gradativa.

Ao todo, mais de 60 localidades, entre bairros e condomínios, foram afetadas pelo desabastecimento.

articles.title: Vídeo mostra discurso de Cleitinho antes de passar mal no Senado | G1
articles.standfirst: Durante a fala, o senador criticou a postura do atual governador, o aumento da previsão de déficit nas contas públicas do estado para 2027 e se emociou ao agradecer ao pai e irmão que já faleceram.
articles.summary: Durante a fala, o senador criticou a postura do atual governador, o aumento da previsão de déficit nas contas públicas do estado para 2027 e se emociou ao agradecer ao pai e irmão.
articles.body:
Um vídeo registrado durante uma sessão no Senado Federal mostra o discurso do governador eleito de Minas Gerais, Cleitinho Azevedo (Republicanos), momentos antes de ele passar mal, na tarde desta quinta-feira (15) . Durante a fala, o senador criticou a postura do atual governador, Mateus Simões, dizendo que falta "humildade". Cleitinho também falou sobre o aumento da previsão de déficit nas contas públicas do estado para 2027. ( Veja no vídeo acima ).

Em seu discurso, o governador eleito também se emocionou ao falar que essa "possa ter sido sua última fala no Senado" e afirmou que tinha tomado alguns remédios e, por isso, estava "um pouco eufórico".

"Não posso deixar de agradecer ao povo mineiro, ao meu pai, que não está aqui mais. Ao meu irmão Mateus que faleceu durante esse processo de eleição. A minha família, aos meus assessores. Tenho certeza que vou colocar pessoas melhores do que eu, para governarmos juntos", completou.

Após o discurso, Cleitinho precisou ser atendido pela equipe de saúde do Senado, com queixa de mal-estar.

Segundo nota do Serviço Médico de Emergência da Casa, ele apresentou um pico de pressão arterial e frequência cardíaca um pouco elevada. O senador passou por exames de eletrocardiograma e enzimas cardíacas, que apresentaram resultados normais.

Após receber medicação e hidratação, ele apresentou melhora e foi liberado com orientação de repouso.

Antes de ser atendido, o senador discursou sobre a transição de governo e criticou o aumento da previsão de déficit nas contas de MG para 2027, de R$ 8,87 bilhões para R$ 10,51 bilhões.

A revisão foi e ncaminhada por Mateus Simões à Assembleia Legislativa nesta quarta-feira (14) , por meio de uma alteração no projeto da Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA).

"Que preparo é esse pelo estado? Que até então, antes, na campanha, o estado estava mil maravilhas. Agora, a partir de 1º de janeiro, o estado quebrou?", questionou Cleitinho.

O governador eleito também afirmou que fará uma auditoria e revisará os contratos do estado quando assumir o cargo.

"Qualquer coisa que você for fazer achando que vai me prejudicar, Mateus, você não vai me prejudicar. Você vai prejudicar a população mineira. Você disse que tinha medo de eu ganhar a eleição de deixar o estado quebrado, falido. E você disse agora que talvez em janeiro já não tenha dinheiro para pagar os servidores. Vocês reclamaram isso do PT durante oito anos, e vocês estão deixando o estado da mesma maneira que o PT deixou", afirmou.

Em 4 de outubro, após vencer as eleições, Cleitinho chegou a declarar que pretendia convidar Simões a permanecer no governo.

Procurado pelo g1, o governo de Minas Gerais afirmou, em nota, que a atual gestão mantém o compromisso com a transparência e as contas públicas.

"É de conhecimento público a delicada situação fiscal do Estado de Minas Gerais, herdada em 2019 pela atual gestão. Desde 2019, medidas gerais de contenção de gastos e ampliação das receitas foram executadas de forma decisiva, o que permitiu o equilíbrio das contas públicas nos últimos anos. Prova do sucesso dessa estratégia de reequilíbrio é que as despesas de pessoal comparadas à Receita Corrente Líquida (RCL) saíram de 66,65% de comprometimento em 2018, no Governo anterior, para os atuais 48,80%, conforme último relatório fiscal publicado", informou a nota.

A atual gestão do Governo de Minas reafirma seu compromisso com a transparência e com as contas públicas, sempre tendo em vista o bem-estar coletivo e o interesse público. Todas as obras públicas e empresas sempre foram auditadas pelos órgãos responsáveis e os documentos seguem à disposição das autoridades competentes.

Da mesma forma, o processo de transição de Governo foi iniciado em 6 de outubro, de maneira transparente e profissional. É conduzido em conformidade com as exigências legais, incluindo as publicações realizadas no Diário Oficial de Minas Gerais, com acesso a todos os cidadãos mineiros. Conforme já informado, as reuniões entre a comissão e os integrantes do Governo serão transmitidas ao vivo e online nos canais das redes sociais e no canal Rede Minas 2. Mais informações:

É de conhecimento público a delicada situação fiscal do Estado de Minas Gerais, herdada em 2019 pela atual gestão. Desde 2019, medidas gerais de contenção de gastos e ampliação das receitas foram executadas de forma decisiva, o que permitiu o equilíbrio das contas públicas nos últimos anos. Prova do sucesso dessa estratégia de reequilíbrio é que as despesas de pessoal comparadas à Receita Corrente Líquida (RCL) saíram de 66,65% de comprometimento em 2018, no Governo anterior, para os atuais 48,80%, conforme último relatório fiscal publicado.

Sobre o Projeto de Lei Orçamentária Anual (PLOA 2027), é preciso reforçar que se trata de previsão, que não necessariamente irá ocorrer. Nos últimos cinco anos (entre 2021 e 2025), houve superávit das contas. A título de exemplo, o superávit de 2025 foi de R$ 1,108 bilhão, sendo que a LOA do mesmo ano previa um déficit de R$ 8,6 bilhões. Caberá ao futuro governo fazer os ajustes que julgar adequados, como o atual governo fez. Por referência, o Governo de São Paulo apresentou déficit efetivo no mesmo período, mesmo sendo considerado o modelo de excelência em gestão financeira pelo Governo eleito.

Por fim, já foi informado que o salário referente a dezembro de 2026, com pagamento previsto para janeiro de 2027, será depositado até 6 de janeiro. O 13º salário também será pago integralmente ainda em 2026, em data a ser divulgada em breve. Desde agosto de 2021, os salários dos servidores do Poder Executivo estadual são pagos integralmente até o quinto dia útil de cada mês, com antecipação em algumas ocasiões. Essa regularidade será mantida até o encerramento da atual gestão.

articles.title: Gabriel Rufián rompe su silencio: "Ayer estuve a punto de irme, me frenaron; he fracasado, hemos fracasado"
articles.standfirst: El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso analiza la actualidad política y las alianzas de izquierdas
articles.summary: El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso analiza la actualidad política y las alianzas de izquierdas
articles.body: Gabriel Rufián, portavoz de ERC en el Congreso de los Diputados, ha roto su silencio tras los últimos acuerdos entre su formación y Podemos de cara a las elecciones generales. El dirigente catalán se había pronunciado en redes sociales sobre las alianzas de izquierdas de cara a las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre, pero no de forma tan amplia como en la entrevista a RAC1. El dirigente ha confesado su hartazgo tras las negociaciones con las formaciones de izquierda: "He tenido semanas mejores y también peores. Ayer estuve a punto de irme, me frenaron. No rajaré de nadie porque el culebrón que damos entre todos y todas es nefasto. Estoy por la gente de ERC y más allá, gente que me coja por el cuello y me dice, ni de coña. Si no, me iría a casa, porque me da mucha pereza". Este viernes, a las 00:00 horas, termina el plazo para presentar las coaliciones. No se descartan pactos sobre la bocina. Gabriel Rufián, sin embargo, ha confesado que su proyecto inicial de unir a las izquierdas, casi con total seguridad, no se podrá llevar a cabo: "Pido disculpas a la gente porque yo llegué a pensar que repitiendo lo que se decía en la calle, yo no me inventé nada, y en base a mi fuerza, con toda la humildad posible, podía arrastrar a los aparatos de los partidos. Y probablemente no pueda. He fracasado. Hemos fracasado. Quedan horas, pero es muy probable que no pase". El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso de los Diputados ha valorado positivamente el acuerdo con Podemos, con Irene Montero al frente: "Me hubiera gustado un frente real. Una serie de cosas que probablemente no se puedan hacer. El acuerdo con Podemos me parece positivo, he hecho todo lo que he podido para simplificar la oferta electora de las izquierdas". Por otra parte, Gabriel Rufián ha criticado al PSOE y a Pedro Sánchez, del que ha apuntado que ha preferido convocar elecciones con el marco de la vivienda y no con el de Ceuta por proteger su figura: "El PSOE cree que pueda salvar la papeleta electoral si queda primero. No sumar, quedar primero". En cuanto a Ada Colau, candidata de Frente Amplio, Rufián sólo ha tenido "buenas palabras" hacia ella, aunque ha apuntado que, como él, no ha tenido la capacidad para arrastrar a los partidos a una entente. El portavoz de ERC ha afirmado que nunca se ha planteado dejar su actual partido para formar parte de Frente Amplio. "Mi trabajo es posicionar a ERC en un lugar ganador, no alimentar ni cuidar el ego de nadie o evitar que alguien se enfade", ha comentado. Además, Gabriel Rufián ha insistido en que el proyecto de Frente Amplio, tal como está planteado, es otra versión de Sumar: "El plan no es liderar la izquierda española". Gabriel Rufián no ha escondido que la, parece, complicada consolidación de un frente de izquierdas es "una guerra de egos". "Todo el mundo tiene ego, pero es como el colesterol, hay colesterol bueno y colesterol malo", ha comentado con humor. "El partido que dice Madrid es mío es Más Madrid y eso cierra la puerta a Podemos", ha señalado. El portavoz de ERC ha insistido en que el proyecto planteado por Frente Amplio es simplemente un cambio de siglas.

articles.title: Personal attacks fly as Sullivan, Peltola spar over corruption, character and controversy
articles.summary: Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola traded sharp attacks over corruption, staffing allegations and military spending in their fiery final Alaska Senate debate.
articles.body: Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola traded blows Thursday night in the final debate of a Senate race that has surprised some political observers with how close it has become. The latest Fox News Power Rankings rate Alaska’s Senate race as a "toss-up," meaning neither party has an edge. Alaska has historically favored the GOP, though the party’s margin of victory has narrowed in recent cycles. Sullivan and Peltola clashed over energy costs, the Iran war, Social Security reform, healthcare policy, military spending, allegations of misconduct and fish, among other topics, but a handful of exchanges stood out from the rest. GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING ‘You must be getting dizzy up here’ Throughout the debate, Peltola attacked Sullivan for being a D.C. insider and using his position to enrich himself and his allies. Sullivan attempted to rebut her claims by pointing to Peltola’s extensive lobbying career after her time in office, accusing her of cashing in by selling influence. "My opponent keeps talking about corporate greed again; she defines the rigged system in D.C.," Sullivan said. "There's nothing more rigged than a member of Congress getting fired and then immediately walking through the revolving door to cash in. She made almost half a million last year as a D.C. lobbyist selling her knowledge of D.C. She did it when she left the state legislature; she set up a lobbying firm." "You're walking through the revolving door so much, you must be getting dizzy up here," he quipped. Peltola responded by saying that her lobbying work was done to benefit Alaskans and highlighting how Sullivan has gotten wealthier since coming to Washington. "Dan's been in D.C. for 12 years and gotten richer every single one of those years. That's the corruption that Alaskans are really sick of, and that's the corruption that I'll fight against. Dan went to D.C. with $3 million. He now has $8 million," she said. "Dan's doing just fine watching out for himself." ‘Questions beforehand?’ After Peltola responded to a question about how she would work to improve affordability for Alaskans if elected to the Senate while appearing to read from a piece of paper, Sullivan questioned whether she had received a copy of the debate questions in advance. "Here's a moderator question, we weren't supposed to get these questions beforehand, were we?" Sullivan asked. "No, sir," one moderator responded. "Neither one of you got questions beforehand," the other moderator said. "Absolutely not." CARVILLE MOCKS DEM CANDIDATE STAFFERS AS 'WEAK' AND 'SOFT' FOR COMPLAINING ABOUT TREATMENT TO NEW YORK TIMES "I'm just watching my opponent read questions that seem to be answered," the senator said. ‘Let's have some decorum’ After Sullivan brought up a New York Times report airing complaints from anonymous staffers alleging that Peltola physically and verbally mistreated her employees, the Democrat lashed out at the incumbent senator, prompting moderators to interject. "Look, my opponent has been telling lies throughout this entire campaign, and it's revealed character challenges. But it's not just the lies. Take a look at how she treats Alaskans when the cameras are off," Sullivan said. "Look at that New York Times story. She treats young Alaskans horribly. 25 staffers quit on Mary Peltola because she abused them physically and emotionally, and then she slanders every other group — African Americans, special needs individuals. It is a character flaw of my opponent." Sullivan’s statement prompted Peltola to attempt to cut him off, calling the reports "gossip" and "unfounded." "Let's have some decorum here," a moderator said, after Peltola began to interrupt Sullivan, who was speaking past his allotted time. Though Peltola’s campaign disputed several of the allegations, including claims that she used slurs and shoved a young staffer, her spokesman said some of her behavior came during a period of extreme grief after the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. DEM SENATE HOPEFUL RACKED UP HUNDREDS OF MISSED VOTES DURING STOPS AT MULTIPLE TAXPAYER SERVING JOBS SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER ‘Lying and the dishonesty’ Another heated moment came after Sullivan accused Peltola of blocking pay for members of the armed services over access to transgender medical procedures. "My opponent did vote against our military, did vote against pay raise for our troops, because she wanted more transgender surgeries for our troops. I mean, that is an outrage," the senator said. "I need to rebut that, that is absurd," Peltola interjected. "Yeah. I think that Alaskans have had it up to here with the lying and the dishonesty. Dan, you should be ashamed of yourself for propagating these lies," the Democrat responded. "The first time I voted on the NDAA, there was trick language in there that would have prohibited our soldiers from getting health care that they needed if they were not stationed in a state that didn't allow for women's reproductive health care. I'm not doing that to our soldiers. But three other times I voted hard yes, in support of our troops." ‘One nice thing’ Near the end of the debate, each candidate was asked to say one nice thing about their opponent. "Well, my wife invited Mary to attend my Marine Corps retirement ceremony after 30 years, and they honored me, but they honored my wife and daughters more than anybody at my retirement ceremony … and Mary Peltola attended, so I thank her for that," Sullivan said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Yeah, that was a lovely, lovely service. And I was so proud to be there. And one, you know, three wonderful attributes of Dan and Julie are their lovely daughters. So that's three lovely things I can say about Dan and Julie," said Peltola.

articles.title: Personal jabs, billionaire donors and party loyalty fuel heated Maine Senate debate
articles.summary: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson clashed over political independence and billionaire donors in their fourth Maine Senate debate before the Nov. 3 election.
articles.body: Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson clashed over billionaire donors, party loyalty and working-class voters Thursday night as their fourth debate took a notably personal turn. In the debate's top moments, Jackson needled Collins over whether she had meaningfully pushed back on Republican-led decisions she disagreed with. Collins defended her record and questioned whether Jackson would stand up to his own party when pursuing the best interests of Maine. COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME' Jackson tells Collins to ‘shut up’ When a heckler interrupted the debate and began shouting about data centers and climate change, Collins said the man was "obviously one of Troy's supporters." "Oh shut up," Jackson shot back. "I don't even know that kid." Campaign donations and campaign promises Near the beginning of the night, Collins questioned whether Jackson had really kept campaign promises to reject billionaire donors that aligned themselves closely with his and other Democratic campaigns, noting FEC contribution records that seemed to clash with those assurances. "And as far as the billionaires that I might have on my campaign, that is accurate," Jackson admitted. "But I haven't … " Jackson paused for a moment as members of the crowd gave an audible reaction to the admission. MAINE DEM SEN CANDIDATE'S 'WORKING CLASS' CRED SHREDDED BY BOTH PARTIES WHEN INTERNET SEES LATEST 'CRINGEY' AD "I haven’t made any deals like Senator Collins has with those billionaires," he continued. "I’m going to tax those billionaires when I get to the U.S. Senate." Jackson did not specify what agreements he was referring to. WATCH: MAINE'S JACKSON ADMITS HAVING BILLIONAIRE DONORS DESPITE PROMISING TO REJECT THEIR MONEY: Jackson questions Collins' independence from Trump and GOP Collins also faced questions about her independence from President Donald Trump. At one point, the moderator asked her to identify an instance when she had defied the president and changed the outcome of a decision. Collins cited her opposition to the confirmation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who faced scrutiny during his nomination over his qualifications and allegations about his personal conduct. "At one point, I had organized people to vote against Secretary Hegseth. As you undoubtedly have read, at the very last minute, one of our Republicans changed his mind. Otherwise, he would have been defeated for that job," Collins said. Jackson countered that Hegseth was ultimately confirmed despite Collins' opposition. "Senator Collins likes to have it both ways. I mean, the reality is that 100% of the time when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there. That has happened time and time again," Jackson said. FORMER OBAMA ADVISOR TELLS DIVIDED MAINE DEMOCRATS TO 'GET OVER YOUR S---' AND WIN THE RACE Meanwhile, Collins pointed to what she described as a "major difference between Troy and me. I vote very independently ... I am the most bipartisan member of the Senate." And referring to Jackson, Collins said, "We don’t need more people who are going to vote a straight party line." Jackson defended his own independence by pointing to clashes with Democratic Maine Gov. Janet Mills during his tenure in the state Senate. "How can I be a rubber stamp with my very own governor — a Democratic governor — vetoing 40 of my bills?" Jackson asked. Jackson had repeatedly challenged Collins over her voting record in their three prior debates. Collins disputed his characterization of her record, arguing that he had overstated how frequently she sided with Trump. "You have heard Troy say that I vote with the president 92 or 94% of the time; that takes only a third of the votes. If you look at 90% of the votes, you will find that I vote with him 72% of the time, not 95% of the time," Collins said. Jackson takes personal swing at Collins with 'working class' dig The debate took a personal turn near the end when Jackson, a former logger, questioned whether Collins looked down on him because of his working-class background. "You know, you said consistently that I don't have the experience. You just said it tonight that I wouldn't be able to do the things that you do. Growing up as a working-class person, I have all kinds of experience," Jackson said. "And so, I guess, you know, what I'm curious about — is it just me that you look down on, or is it working-class people overall?" Collins rejected the accusation and pointed to her own working-class roots. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Troy, I do not look down on you or on anyone. I grew up in Caribou. My first job was picking potatoes," Collins said. "I have worked since I was age ten, literally since I was age ten. I have enormous respect for all the people of Maine." The debate came as Collins and Jackson entered the home stretch of the campaign ahead of Maine's Nov. 3 general election, with control of the U.S. Senate at stake.

articles.title: Illegal alien busted allegedly hauling enough fentanyl to potentially kill state’s entire population — twice
articles.summary: A routine speeding stop on a Nevada highway allegedly uncovered over 700 pounds of fentanyl and methamphetamine — enough to kill millions, prosecutors say.
articles.body: An illegal immigrant pulled over for speeding in Nevada allegedly had enough fentanyl in his truck to kill millions, federal prosecutors say. Francisco Joel Garcia Farias, 26, now faces federal drug-trafficking charges after a Lincoln County sheriff’s deputy stopped his pickup on a rural highway and a narcotics detection dog alerted to the vehicle, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Nevada. Inside, authorities say they found 13 large storage totes packed with approximately 30 pounds of suspected fentanyl and 677 pounds of suspected methamphetamine, a combined haul of more than 700 pounds. CALIFORNIA K-9 OTIS HELPS POLICE SEIZE 440 POUNDS OF COCAINE DURING ALHAMBRA TRAFFIC STOP "The massive scale of this seizure underscores the staggering volume of illicit narcotics flowing into our communities from transnational criminal organizations," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. "Fourteen kilograms of fentanyl alone represents approximately seven million potentially lethal two-milligram doses — enough to kill more than twice the population of Nevada — and, when combined with over 650 pounds of methamphetamine, represents an estimated street value of approximately $2 million," Chattah said. AS A US ATTORNEY, I SEE FENTANYL'S HORRIFYING TOLL UP CLOSE. CONGRESS MUST ACT NOW Based on that lethal-dose estimate, the fentanyl could potentially kill nearly twice the population of Los Angeles, everyone in Indiana or roughly the entire population of Paraguay. "These staggering quantities reflect a blatant disregard for human life, driven purely by profit," Chattah said. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF FENTANYL DEALING LINKED TO VIRGINIA HIGH SCHOOL OVERDOSES The Justice Department identified Garcia Farias as an illegal immigrant in its announcement of the charges. The bust began Oct. 13 on U.S. Highway 93 near Ash Springs, Nevada, where a deputy saw the pickup traveling above the posted speed limit, according to prosecutors’ account of the criminal complaint. HERO K-9 SNIFFS OUT HIDDEN $6M COCAINE SHIPMENT ALONG US-CANADA BORDER After the dog alerted, deputies searched the truck and uncovered numerous vacuum-sealed packages inside the totes. Authorities recovered approximately 187 packages of a white crystalline substance weighing about 307.22 kilograms, along with 13 brick-shaped packages weighing approximately 14 kilograms. Field tests of selected samples were positive for methamphetamine and fentanyl, respectively, prosecutors said. DOJ ANNOUNCES 81 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS INDICTED AFTER PUERTO RICO DRUG TRAFFICKING TAKEDOWN U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the seizure kept a potentially deadly drug supply off American streets. "Anyone who plans to release a deadly drug like fentanyl onto American streets will be prosecuted," Blanche said. "Thanks to the diligent work of federal and local law enforcement, the lethal drugs allegedly possessed by this illegal alien are no longer endangering the lives of countless Americans." CBP OFFICERS SEIZE $67 MILLION IN ILLEGAL DRUGS AT SAN DIEGO BORDER PORTS, DHS SAYS The investigation involved Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office and Homeland Security Task Force partners. "The suspected fentanyl and methamphetamine seized in this case represent an extraordinary threat to public safety," said John A. Condon, executive associate director of HSI. "Through close coordination with the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, the U.S. Attorney’s Office and our Homeland Security Task Force partners, HSI will continue to identify, investigate and hold accountable those who profit from poisoning Americans and endangering our communities," Condon said. Lincoln County Sheriff Derek Foremaster credited his deputies’ traffic enforcement and the trained dog with uncovering the suspected narcotics. DOJ TOUTS HUNDREDS OF GUN, DRUG ARRESTS AS ST LOUIS SURGE OPERATION ENDS: 'VIOLENCE IS NOT INEVITABLE' "The allegations in this case underscore the serious threat illicit narcotics pose to rural communities and the traveling public," Foremaster said. "I am proud of the vigilance and professionalism demonstrated by our deputies, whose proactive traffic enforcement and trained K-9 deployment led to the identification of suspected narcotics and a coordinated response with Homeland Security Investigations." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Garcia Farias is charged with possession with intent to distribute 400 grams or more of a mixture containing fentanyl and possession with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of a mixture containing methamphetamine. If convicted, he faces a mandatory minimum of 10 years in prison and a maximum of life on each count, followed by five years of supervised release, according to prosecutors.

articles.title: Trump won over Gen Z in 2024. Can the GOP win them back?
articles.summary: Democrats are winning over Generation Z by a wide margin ahead of November’s midterms, a trend that sailed in the opposite direction when President Trump won in 2024 over former Vice President Kamala Harris. A big reason is the underlying theme of the 2026 midterms that has been hitting the GOP hard across demographic lines:…
articles.body:
Democrats are winning over Generation Z by a wide margin ahead of November’s midterms, a trend that sailed in the opposite direction when President Trump won in 2024 over former Vice President Kamala Harris.

A big reason is the underlying theme of the 2026 midterms that has been hitting the GOP hard across demographic lines: affordability and the economy.

“The numbers are very clear right now on Gen Z leaning hard Democratic, and a lot of that is tied to the White House and how chaotic the cost-of-living picture still feels,” said Rina Shah, a political strategist and founder of Vental Strategic Advisory Group.

A New York Times and Siena University poll conducted in September found that Democrats are winning over voters between the ages of 18 and 29 by 35 points.

Shah said Republicans need to tell “a more clear story on economic mobility.”

“Candidates who do that authentically, and who treat Gen Z as voters who might actually be persuadable rather than a lost cause, can close the gap,” Shah said. “Age helps, fluency online helps, but the substance on costs and opportunity is what decides whether the attention converts into votes.”

Some say several young Democratic recruits may be helping the party win over Gen Z in the battle for the Senate. These candidates include 39-year-old Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.), who is running for reelection, as well as Texas Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico, 37, and Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, 41.

“Those three [Ossoff, Talarico and El-Sayed] are effective for very different reasons, and Republicans should pay attention instead of dismissing them,” Shah said.

Yemisi Egbewole, a political strategist and former chief of staff and adviser to the Biden White House Press Office, said the Democratic Party has a “blessing” of having a “good slate of rising stars” who are very relatable to younger generations.

But he also said Republicans have people in their party to look at when it comes to winning over younger voters. Egbewole cited Texas Rep. Brandon Gill and Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds as two politicians focusing on “young” campaign strategies.

“He [Gill] is somebody that I definitely see is a rising star in the GOP and when I think about who can fight for young people’s attention,” Egbewole told The Hill.

Socialism, and the drift among younger voters toward candidates espousing left-wing, democratic socialist views, may also be a problem for the GOP with Gen Z.

“If the GOP thinks that socialism and its temptations are just a far left issue, they’re going to be very, very surprised when more young people start looking as socialism as the alternative to the life that they were promised,” Egbewole said.

Young voters are keenly focused on housing and general affordability when it comes to politics.

But Rachel Janfaza, founder of the Gen Z-focused media and strategy firm The Up and Up, believes younger people’s concerns aren’t too different from those of older generations.

“I don’t think that the [GOP campaign] tactics have to be that drastically different when you’re talking to younger and older voters,” Janfaza told The Hill. “Young people don’t want to be talked down to, they don’t want to feel like politicians are pandering for their votes.”

Janfaza believes this isn’t a new problem for Republicans and that the party’s relatability problem with Gen Z needs a solution.

“When you have Trump saying that affordability doesn’t exist, or that it isn’t a problem, that certainly rubs the wrong way, because it exists for them,” Janfaza said.

Gen Z is running for Congress. But where are the women?

Millennials and Generation Z now make up a third of congressional candidates, but men outnumber women 3-to-1.

That gap is widest among Gen Z, where more than 80 percent of candidates are male, according to Future Caucus .

Layla Zaidane, the president and CEO of Future Caucus, suggested rising political violence and institutional barriers are two explanations for the gender gap.

“One hypothesis is that we’re seeing candidates and public servants enter a political environment that has been plagued by political violence and often that hostility and aggression and violence is targeted toward women more than men,” Zaidane told The Hill.

“And so it’s not hard to imagine if you’re a Gen Z young woman, considering if you want to put yourself or potentially your family through that, that it just doesn’t seem like the juice is worth the squeeze,” she added.

Women also face structural barriers to entering politics, particularly at the state level, where low pay can make childcare unaffordable and government buildings often lack family-friendly facilities.

“I just think there are some logistical concerns that make it a tough pill to swallow for a young woman who is thinking about doing this,” Zaidane said.

“A lot of legislative buildings or state capitals don’t have bathrooms with changing tables or rooms for, you know, if you had to feed your child,” she explained. “We have a state lawmaker in Vermont — they don’t even have offices in Vermont — and she had a baby and was like, ‘Do you just go into a public bathroom and sit there to feed?’”

The CEO also pointed to Rep. Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.), who was pregnant in 2025 and alongside Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) sought to change congressional rules to allow proxy voting for new parents.

“Today marks the first day I am unable to fly to DC for votes due to travel restrictions ahead of my due date,” the Colorado lawmaker wrote in a January 2025 post to social platform X.

“It shouldn’t be this way. Congress must pass my bipartisan resolution to allow Members who are new parents to vote remotely,” Pettersen added.

The procedural rule failed to garner enough support.

“I think having more women helps make that balance a little bit more reflective of what it’s like to live in America,” Zaidane said.

She recalled a colleague who worked for a congressman who voted against legislation requiring changing tables in public buildings. The colleague, who had recently given birth, relied on her husband to bring their baby to work so she could feed and care for the child. While the need for changing tables was obvious to her, the congressman had focused primarily on the cost to taxpayers.

Electing more women and younger lawmakers could help modernize Congress and remove those barriers, whose institutional practices were established when its members came from far less diverse backgrounds.

“[The] institution was designed, you know, a really long time ago when everybody who served in Congress kind of looked the same and had the same background,” Zaidane said.

“Adapting and modernizing and making sure that women, young people, et cetera, can bring some of what would make the Congress feel more dynamic and alive and modern —I think those are things that we really need,” she added.

“More women, more Gen Zers, more new people to step into office in order to push those ideas forward.”

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: Republicans have been irrationally exuberant about Hispanic voters. It may cost them
articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!] Here’s a midterm microcosm for you: National Republicans are…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ]

Here’s a midterm microcosm for you: National Republicans are pulling out of the effort to defeat Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar (Texas) in a district that runs from south of San Antonio all along the Rio Grande.

It was an ill omen then that the same day the party was cutting its losses there, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) visited the district next door and, appearing with Cuellar’s Republican challenger, announced: “South Texas will literally decide the majority in the country.”

It’s been a week of sail trimming for Republicans, with Washington even pulling the plug on a couple of incumbent House members. Given the massive cash advantage that the GOP has wielded so ostentatiously throughout the cycle, kissing off sitting members is a marker of serious panic for the party in power.

But it’s Texas that’s been, ahem, deep in the heart of Republicans’ vision for a this-time-is-different kind of midterm cycle.

Cuellar’s district was a prime target in the GOP’s gerrymandering effort that kicked off the coast-to-coast redistricting battle. Republican lawmakers in Austin nudged Cuellar’s longtime constituency about 3 points to the right, based on 2024 numbers. President Trump won the old district with 53 percent of the vote. He would have won the new district with 55 percent. But Cuellar, whom Trump even tried to get to switch parties with a presidential pardon, seems to be having a smooth ride to reelection as a Democrat.

The district, Texas’s 28th, was one of 13 across the country in which voters preferred Trump for president but chose Democrats for the House. Back in the heady days of the early 2025 “vibe shift,” these were the districts in which Republicans claimed would allow them to actually expand their skinny majority in midterms. Granted, that’s mostly just stuff people say. It’s not like party leaders can start their candidate recruitment and fundraising drive saying, “We’re probably heading for the minority, but your millions could help save a few seats here and there.” But Republicans may have been more serious than the typical midterm bloviators. And that’s because of Texas — Hispanic Texas particularly.

Another of those 13 split-ticket districts is right next door to Cuellar’s: the already swing-y 34th, where a similar 3-point gerrymander nudge was supposed to knock out Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas). Gonzales doesn’t look like a lock yet, but certainly he’s favored to win in a climate that just keeps improving for Democrats in the closing weeks. (In fact, of the original 13 targets by the National Republican Campaign Committee, only one — Maine’s 2nd — is rated as a GOP lean. Eleven are blue, and one — North Carolina’s 1st — is a toss-up.)

But Republicans weren’t just imagining their 2026 opportunity, especially in South Texas. Nationwide, Hispanic voters swung 8 points to the right from 2020 to 2024, with 43 percent backing Trump’s bid for a second term, which was even higher than the previous modern record for Republicans with Hispanic voters: former President George W. Bush ’s 35 percent in 2000. And Texas led the charge.

Webb County, home to Laredo, is the southern anchor of Cuellar’s district. It’s big, with a population of nearly 300,000, and at least 95 percent of its residents are Hispanic. It’s also prosperous, with the highest household income of any of Texas’s Hispanic-majority counties. And it was overwhelmingly Democratic. In 2012 and 2016, Democratic presidential candidates won Webb by more than 50 points.

It should have been alarming to Democrats then when in 2020 as the party was running well ahead of its 2016 performance, Webb County saw its Democratic vote share almost cut in half. That 20-point decline wasn’t the floor, either. In 2024, the Republican presidential candidate carried Webb County for the first time since former President William Howard Taft in 1912. A Democratic stronghold that had survived landslides in 1952, 1956, 1972 and 1984 collapsed in the relatively close 2024 contest. Opinions vary on the principal cause, but some combination of anger at the high cost of living and disorder at the U.S.-Mexico border are the conventional culprits. But, Republicans wondered if it wasn’t something deeper and that a larger realignment among Hispanic voters was underway.

The national polling we have about Hispanic voters’ attitudes this cycle says that the relationship between the GOP and Latinos has reverted to pre-2024 levels, with 35 percent preferring Republican control of Congress. That’s not as low as it was in the Obama era, so there are some likely long-term gains for the red team. But it’s certainly at least back to where the party started at the outset of the Trump era.

Of course, Hispanic voters aren’t a national constituency any more than white voters are. Hispanic voters in California are very different from those in Arizona, who are very different from those in Florida, who are very different from those in New York and Texas, and so on. One’s political affiliation tends to have more to do with geography, marital status, income, educational attainment, etc., than one’s surname. Indeed, Democrats’ tendency to treat Hispanic voters as monolithic and obsessed with lenient immigration policies helps explain some of the party’s slide since the 2010s.

But Republicans seem to have made a similar error in reverse by failing to see how a group, especially in working-class south Texas, would be sensitive to high consumer prices. Or how a group that lamented a chaotic situation at the border would similarly dislike overbroad, aggressive internal enforcement that often appears to be ethnic profiling.

Part of the reason Republicans are pulling money from other races right now is that the Texas gerrymandering bid that was supposed to grow the GOP majority has turned into a colossally expensive proposition . Texas is a costly place to run elections under good circumstances, but a hellaciously pricey one if you’re fighting the tide.

Republicans might have saved themselves money, time and trouble if instead of focusing on the big 2024 swing, they had looked a little deeper. In the previous two midterm cycles, Webb County stayed very Democratic. In 2018, when former Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D-Texas) was chasing Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), Webb County came in for the Democrat 71 percent to 28 percent. That doesn’t mean that Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is guaranteed to replicate that kind of performance, but it would have been good for Republicans to have at least considered in the crazy days of 2025.

articles.title: How DOJ hopes the Supreme Court will limit judges’ authority next
articles.summary: The Trump administration is making its next move to rein in judges’ authority to block the president’s agenda. On Wednesday, the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to declare that judges can’t set aside federal agency rules nationwide when they find them unlawful. It would add to the Trump administration’s major high court victory two…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is making its next move to rein in judges’ authority to block the president’s agenda.

On Wednesday, the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to declare that judges can’t set aside federal agency rules nationwide when they find them unlawful.

It would add to the Trump administration’s major high court victory two years ago clawing back nationwide injunctions .

But this round, the president faces a steeper climb.

When the Biden administration tried advancing the argument, Chief Justice John Roberts slapped it down as “fairly radical.” Justice Brett Kavanaugh called it “far-reaching.”

But three other conservative justices have expressed sympathy, and the Trump administration hopes it’ll be able to lay the groundwork for a majority that hands the president another win.

The battle revolves around the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which governs lawsuits challenging the vast array of regulations across the federal government. It instructs judges to “hold unlawful and set aside agency action” they find to be “arbitrary, capricious,” unconstitutional or otherwise exceeding the agency’s power.

For years, judges have interpreted that language to mean they can block actions nationwide. It’s become a cornerstone of many of the most consequential lawsuits stymieing presidential administration actions.

No surprise, presidents from both parties aren’t fans.

“The Biden administration and the Obama administration, especially toward the end, got caught up in a lot of a lot of litigation challenging their priorities,” said Molly Nixon, a senior fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute who researches executive power. “They didn’t like it the same way that the Trump administration doesn’t like it.”

When Elizabeth Prelogar, former President Biden’s top Supreme Court lawyer, raised the argument to the justices during a 2022 argument, it earned her a grilling from the chief justice.

“How many cases would you say that we have issued over the past year, decade, whatever, where we have upheld decisions vacating agency rulings under the APA?” Roberts asked. “Thousands?”

She acknowledged the longstanding practice but stood firm. Prelogar didn’t get far.

“No, no,” Roberts cut in. “Sometimes? Over and over and over again.”

The court’s opinion didn’t address the issue, and Roberts didn’t say anything more about it when it landed.

But he isn’t the only conservative on the court to suggest the practice may be OK.

The next year, Kavanaugh penned a solo takedown of the argument, calling it a “crusade.”

“The Government’s position would revolutionize long-settled administrative law—shutting the door on entire classes of everyday administrative law cases. The Government’s newly minted position is both novel and wrong,” he wrote.

For Kavanaugh and Roberts, they’ve seen the longstanding practice firsthand. They both served on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit — the epicenter of APA suits —before their nominations to the Supreme Court.

“Those of us who were on the D.C. Circuit — five times before breakfast, that’s what you do in an APA case,” Roberts quipped back at the 2022 argument.

It hasn’t seemed to convince all his colleagues.

“Some of us didn’t have the benefit of sitting on the D.C. Circuit five times before breakfast entering these orders,” Gorsuch joked that day. “And I stare at the language.”

The Trump administration says the APA’s instruction to “set aside” agency actions doesn’t give a license to a singular judge to strike down a federal policy in all 50 states.

“As a human being, today, when you set aside something, it’s not the same as striking it,” Nixon explained. “You don’t put a red line through it. You just don’t apply it in that particular case.”

Gorsuch’s doubts were joined by two other conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Amy Coney Barrett, when the court ultimately decided the Biden-era case.

“Color me skeptical,” Gorsuch wrote, saying the court would likely have to address the question “sooner or later.”

Last year, the issue returned to focus again after President Trump returned to office and contested the swarm of nationwide injunctions judges issued blocking his agenda. The Supreme Court sided with him 6-3 along its familiar ideological lines, ruling judges have no authority to issue universal injunctions when federal law doesn’t authorize it.

But the court made clear it wasn’t deciding what that means for the APA.

“Nothing we say today resolves the distinct question,” Barrett wrote for the majority.

If the Trump administration gets the trio’s votes, it would still need two more to form a majority.

That’s where the gambit gets tougher. Even if the administration can persuade Justice Samuel Alito, too, it would still need support from either Roberts or Kavanaugh, assuming the three liberal justices side against Trump.

Alito, for his part, hasn’t signed onto some of his colleagues’ writings on the issue, only saying that invalidating the practice would be a “sea change.”

“I don’t think he’s come down one way or the other, or shown his cards,” Nixon said.

The Trump administration is taking its chances. The justices are likely to consider taking up the case at a closed-door conference later this term.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer warned it’s forcing the administration to “run the table” in every court where it is sued — sometimes all across the country — and more frequently turn to the justices for emergency relief.

“Universal vacatur upends that system, imbuing the orders of courts of first review with the type of nationwide effect usually reserved for the precedents of the court of last resort,” Sauer wrote in the government’s Supreme Court petition this week.

“Universal vacatur has harmful consequences for the courts themselves,” he added.

articles.title: Democrats may be on the cusp of a Senate majority: Here are their top priorities
articles.summary: As Democrats batten down the hatches for a harrowing election night, some are already tossing ideas around about what the first priorities would be in the event they win back the Senate majority. Democrats have about a 56 percent chance of winning the Senate majority in November, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), although they…
articles.body:
As Democrats batten down the hatches for a harrowing election night, some are already tossing ideas around about what the first priorities would be in the event they win back the Senate majority.

Democrats have about a 56 percent chance of winning the Senate majority in November, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), although they still face tall hurdles to getting there. DDHQ forecasts Democrats as having a 77 percent chance of taking the House majority.

If they are successful, they’ll face an administration unfriendly, if not openly hostile, to most of their policy agenda. And they’ll also have a short time period before 2028 jockeying takes over the environment.

That provides risks and rewards for the party.

“It is an opportunity for Democrats to audition for the American people for why they should have complete power after 2028,” said Joshua Miller, government affairs director for Public Citizen, a progressive nonprofit focused on consumers’ rights.

“It’s very easy for the campaign trail to begin to dictate the terms of what happens here in D.C. and I think one of the challenges that they’re going to have to overcome is just ensuring that the agenda that they’re trying to push is helping to set the debate instead of the debate being set for them,” Miller said.

The immediate priority will be oversight of the Trump administration.

With majorities, Democrats will have the power to bring subpoenas and schedule hearings to examine the executive branch’s moves.

Given sharp tensions between the Republican White House and the Democrats in both chambers of Congress, Cabinet secretaries and administration officials are likely to see frequent summons to Capitol Hill for testimony.

But some Democrats are cautioning each other not to lean too much into impeachment efforts, as the Democratic majorities did in the first Trump administration.

Republican leaders have already used this as an attack line . Some candidates, including former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who is leading his comeback race against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), have said they do not support trying to impeach President Trump again. Democratic leaders have been largely noncommittal in either direction.

Phil Gardner, a Democratic strategist and co-founder of Blue Dog Action, a centrist Democratic group, discouraged trying to impeach Cabinet secretaries or, especially, Trump. He said such moves would likely not play well with swing voters.

“If we start to think of 2026 as history repeating itself from 2018, then I don’t have faith that Democrats took lessons from their past defeats or mistakes,” Gardner said, referring to the push for impeachment in 2018 even after then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) threw cold water on the idea at the outset .

“But then again, clearly even some of the people who you know would be ready and eager to impeach Donald Trump do get the fact we did it twice. It didn’t work. It’s probably not going to happen again,” Gardner said.

Democrats in both chambers are likely to make a big push for legislation lowering costs, after spending the whole campaign cycle talking about this chief concern of voters.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) led the caucus in releasing a series of proposals throughout the past year highlighting Trump’s policies that Democrats say have driven costs up and pitching individual bills and broader frameworks for fixing the problem.

“As President Trump mocks affordability as a ‘hoax,’ Senate Democrats have launched a year-long initiative to tackle the high cost of living, focusing on the issues that matter to American families,” reads one of the proposals, which aims to bring down grocery prices by breaking up meatpacker monopolies, among other things.

Healthcare has been a hallmark Democratic priority for decades, and Democrats have already signaled interest in tackling healthcare costs and undoing cuts to Medicaid in the Republicans’ 2025 tax package. Democratic senators also blocked Republican attempts to fund the government last fall over concerns about expiring premium tax credits on Affordable Care Act health plans. Restoring those enhanced tax credits is likely to be high on their priority list.

Wendell Primus, a scholar at the Center for Health Policy at the Brookings Institution, said he expects Democrats to go straight for the Medicaid cuts and the tax credits, although they’ll struggle to get anything past Trump’s desk without making deals. And the looming 2028 election fight could provide an incentive or disincentive to do so.

“It’s a question of, do you try to get something done that may be a little smaller than what you want, because you know you’ve got to deal with a Republican presidency right now, or do you say, ‘We’re going to make a big deal out of this issue, so it helps us, you know, get the ultimate prize, you know, a Democrat president in 2028, or I mean, early 2029,” Primus said.

The playbook that Schumer released in April on healthcare mentions “lower costs,” “reliable care” and “less hassle” as broad tenets of the reforms Democrats want, although it is light on specific legislative approaches. Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is all but certain to be Schumer’s deputy as Democratic whip, has specifically mentioned either delaying or repealing the Medicaid cuts as a No. 2 priority (after ending the Iran war) of a Democratic majority.

“It’s true that that doesn’t actually reduce the rate of inflation, but it does reduce the rate at which people can’t afford their lives,” Schatz told The Washington Sun on Tuesday.

Primus also mentioned reforms to long-term care and drug pricing as potential avenues for healthcare policy in a Democratic majority.

Some House caucuses have released frameworks on specific issues, too, including healthcare, with more specificity.

The New Democrats, a broad coalition of pro-business moderates, released a healthcare action plan last year that lays out priorities including reversing the Medicaid cuts and preserving the tax credits plus cracking down on Medicaid and Medicare fraud, supporting women’s health and bolstering medical research and innovation.

Another policy area likely to be near the top of the to-do list is housing, which could have more robust bipartisan support, unlike many of Democrats’ healthcare goals.

Congress over the summer muscled through a housing package, called the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, that rolled back regulations and created some new programs designed to bring down housing costs, but even that was briefly stalled over tensions with the White House.

Some of those provisions will also need federal funding set aside to go into effect. Dennis Shea, executive vice president for housing at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said he expects bipartisan support for appropriating money to those programs, since many lawmakers have provisions included in the housing bill they want to see come to life.

“I don’t believe HUD [Department ofHousing and Urban Development] will set up these programs, and understandably so, unless there’s some resources put behind them,” Shea said. “So I think that should be priority No. 1 on housing, is to sort of complete the job with ROAD and get the programs established in ROAD funded.”

There are plenty of other policy areas Democrats have their eye on.

Josh Freed, senior vice president for energy policy at Third Way, said he expects interest in permitting reform, which the Senate is set to consider after the elections but that Democrats will likely revive if that effort fails before the holidays.

Freed also mentioned the New Democrats’ energy policy framework , which he called “appropriately ambitious.” Like the Senate permitting deal, several of these policy objectives could have cross-partisan appeal since they focus on cutting down on regulations and addressing grid problems that affect rural areas and red states.

“Most of these things should get 60 votes. Whether they do or not is going to depend on what Republicans are in the Senate and how Donald Trump responds to a Republican minority, and how much the Republicans in the Senate are still listening to him,” Freed said. “So there are a lot of wild cards there that Democrats don’t have much control over, but the actual policy agenda should be able to get six, eight, 10 Republicans to support it.”

Another policy area Democrats are likely to look to is childcare. Several incoming candidates have made childcare costs and access a key part of their platform, and there have been bipartisan efforts this Congress to support the childcare workforce.

Lena Bilik, program manager at Roosevelt Forward, the advocacy arm of the progressive Roosevelt Institute, said the emphasis on childcare as a form of public infrastructure across campaigns and in legislation in recent years is a helpful development. She mentioned several states have adopted sweeping childcare reforms, including New Mexico .

“We’re at a point where we’re seeing an acknowledgement that we have to treat childcare as the economic priority that it is, and as one key that actually can be improved to ease some of the affordability crisis, so I think that’s exciting,” Bilik said. “So obviously, lowering costs-that’s foundational. But it’s exciting to see a focus on supply building, like in this Senate doc , for example, and in other places, and a realization that the childcare workforce is key, so that’s good to see.”

But childcare reforms — especially ambitious ones like universal childcare, which New Mexico has put in place — are likely to face strong headwinds from Republicans. Such moves would also likely need federal funding support, underscoring the need for bipartisan government funding negotiations that balance the budget.

Any of these issues will make for complicated and drawn-out negotiations amid the narrow margins expected from any majority. Miller, from Public Citizen, emphasized that opposing Republicans and Trump is not enough as a guiding platform for Democrats going into next year, and neither is seeking to return to a pre-Trump status quo.

“The bar should not be set at the level, ‘look what the Trump administration is burying, or what they’re doing with you know DHS or DOJ.’ That’s a very low bar,” Miller said, referring to the departments of Homeland Security and Justice. “The bar should be very high in terms of we’re pointing this out because we categorically believe that we are different and will operate differently.”
