articles.title: Confiscation is impossible: Why the entire gun control debate misses the point
articles.summary: Any confiscation program would be analogous to bailing water from a boat with a hole in the hull.
articles.body:
Every few years the American gun debate circles back to the same question: is the Second Amendment an absolute right, or does it allow sweeping restrictions, up to and including taking guns away? Both sides argue as if the answer decides the matter. It doesn’t. Even if the absolutists lost every constitutional argument tomorrow, the government could not confiscate the nation’s firearms. The obstacles are cost, courts, verification and supply, and the attempt would throw away real, unmeasured benefits the country already enjoys.

Start with cost. Americans privately own roughly 500 million firearms , more than one for every man, woman and child in the country. Compensating owners at even $500 per gun would come to about $250 billion, before a single government lawyer, judge or agent is paid or a single warehouse is rented. For comparison, Australia’s 1996 buyback collected about 650,000 guns , less than two-tenths of one percent of the American stockpile.

Then there are the courts. Every contested seizure or valuation becomes a case: takings claims disputing whether compensation was just, Fourth Amendment challenges to searches, and criminal prosecutions of owners who refuse. Tens of millions of Americans own guns . If even a small fraction fought back in court, the result would be hundreds of thousands of cases, each with a right to appeal, landing on a court system that is already backlogged.

As a former counsel for the Florida Department of Revenue, I know what it costs to defend even one contested government action through administrative protest and litigation. The legislation, rulemaking and administration needed to run such a program would only add to that cost. Multiply it across the country, and the machinery of government would simply stop.

Verification may be the hardest problem of all. Federal law has barred a national gun registry since 1986 . The government does not know who owns what, so it cannot know who has complied. In practice, confiscation would depend on voluntary surrender, which is unlikely. The alternative is door-to-door searches, each requiring its own probable cause and the participation of law enforcement, which has more pressing work to do, such as fighting fraud and drug trafficking.

Finally, the guns keep coming. U.S. factories made nearly 10 million firearms in 2023 alone, and the U.S. imported almost 6 million more . Meanwhile, 3D printers and unfinished parts kits now let a hobbyist build a working gun at home. Any confiscation program would be analogous to bailing water from a boat with a hole in the hull. It’s a fool’s errand, and real problems would be neglected while it was being pursued.

The practical case is decisive on its own, but there is also a cost in what we would lose. My degree is in criminology, and criminologists have long known that deterrence works partly through uncertainty. A burglar or carjacker who can’t know whether the homeowner or driver is armed has to weigh that risk, and is likely to be deterred . We don’t track crimes that were never committed, but criminologists know they exist.

The same logic applies internationally. There is a well-worn story that Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto warned against invading the American mainland, in part, because there would be a rifle behind every blade of grass. Whether or not he said it , the reasoning holds. An army can defeat another army, but occupying a country full of armed civilians is a different and far costlier problem, as the U.S. itself learned in Iraq and Afghanistan, and as the British learned from the Minutemen of the American Revolution.

Switzerland and Finland build armed citizens into their national defense. In 2022, Ukraine handed rifles to civilians in Kyiv as Russian columns approached . America’s privately owned arsenal is a standing deterrent that costs taxpayers nothing to maintain. It pays dividends every hour of every day, in the form of invasions never attempted in the minds of would-be conquerors.

The fight over whether the Second Amendment is absolute or can be restricted makes for good legal debate in the courts, a good fundraising issue and good television, but it is beside the point. The cost of confiscating guns is simply prohibitive. Government, the courts and law enforcement would be overwhelmed; compliance could not be verified; and new guns would keep coming in or being made.

Meanwhile, an armed population provides deterrence at home and abroad that no one can fully measure and no one should casually discard. Whatever you think of the Second Amendment, arithmetic and physics have already settled the question of confiscation. The debate should move on to what can actually be done, such as encouraging gun safety training. But that is a debate for another day.

Eric A. de Moya is a licensed Florida attorney and former counsel for the Florida Department of Revenue, where he drafted rules and legislation and helped resolve taxpayer disputes. He holds a B.S. in Criminology from Florida State University.”

articles.title: Rahm Emanuel says Democrats can do a better job linking 2 key issues
articles.summary: Rahm Emanuel thinks Democrats can do a better job linking corruption and affordability concerns ahead of the midterms.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Affordability and fighting corruption are central to the Democrats’ midterm message , but former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel sees the two issues as “heads and tails of the same coin.”

“The president of the United States gets a $450 million gift from Qatar — Air Force One — and you’re getting $4.50 a gallon of gas,” Emanuel said during a recent NewsNation town hall .

Emanuel, who served under the Obama administration, gave Democrats a “B+” for their messaging but thinks they could do a better job connecting affordability and corruption .

“The president is giving them, and Republicans are giving them, an endless amount of material,” he said.

Government corruption topped the list of voter concerns in a recent Fox News survey , with 60 percent saying they were “extremely concerned” about it. Inflation ranked second at 58 percent.

Midterm elections are traditionally a referendum on the party in power, and with Republicans controlling the White House and both chambers of Congress, the GOP is on the defensive .

What are Democrats’ chances of taking the House and Senate?

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill and NewsNation, gives Democrats a 77 percent chance of winning a House majority and a 56 percent chance of taking control of the Senate.

Still, Emanuel doesn’t think a midterm victory would make Democrats a lock to win the White House in 2028.

“The Republicans are going to lose. Democrats aren’t going to win,” he noted, adding that 2027 and “how we comport ourselves will determine whether we have won that year.”

Emanuel urges Democrats to push for ethics reform

The two-term Chicago mayor and former U.S. representative said Democrats have to decide whether the midterms are “transactional” or “transformational” and called for an ethics reform bill that would deliver on the party’s anti-corruption promises.

He urged Democrats to push for legislation that would ban lawmakers from trading stocks and betting on prediction markets and set a mandatory retirement age of 75.

“If all you do is a Democratic version of food fighting, or all you do is investigations with no action … you won’t have delivered change,” Emanuel said.

About half of voters in a recent poll from The Associated Press and NORC Research Center say they want “substantial change,” while roughly 3 in 10 want “complete and total upheaval” in the way the country is run.

The same survey found widespread dissatisfaction with President Trump, but that discontent hasn’t translated into overwhelming enthusiasm for Democrats. About 4 in 10 voters have a “very” or “somewhat” favorable view of Democrats, while about half view the party unfavorably.

Emanuel is currently favored on Kalshi to be the first Democrat to announce a 2028 presidential run.

articles.title: Cook Political Report shifts 11 House seats away from GOP
articles.summary: Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, shifted 11 more House seats toward Democrats this week, many in red states as the midterms inch closer. Cook has moved dozens of House seats away from Republicans in recent weeks as the political environment improves for Democrats, driven by President Trump’s unpopularity in the polls and growing…
articles.body:
Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, shifted 11 more House seats toward Democrats this week, many in red states as the midterms inch closer.

Cook has moved dozens of House seats away from Republicans in recent weeks as the political environment improves for Democrats, driven by President Trump’s unpopularity in the polls and growing disapproval of the Iran war.

Republican Reps. Brad Finstad (Minn.), Mike Turner (Ohio) and Mike Carey (Ohio) saw their districts shift from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.” Two open seats — New York’s 21st Congressional District and South Carolina’s 1st Congressional District — shifted in a similar manner.

GOP Reps. Derek Schmidt (Kan.) and Mike Flood (Neb.) saw their districts move from “safe Republican” to “likely Republican,” as well as an open seat held by the GOP, Florida’s 16th District, according to Cook.

Montana’s open 1st Congressional District, which Trump carried by 12 points in 2024, moved from “lean Republican” to “toss up.”

For the Democrats, incumbent Reps. Greg Landsman (Ohio) and Jared Moskowitz (Fla.) saw their districts move further left. Republicans redrew Landsman’s and Moskowitz’s districts ahead of the midterms and hoped the new maps would make the seats easier to flip.

Unlike in the 2018 midterms, when many of the Democratic gains were in areas former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton won in 2016, the party needs to focus on Trump-won seats to win a sizable House majority this year.

Many of the districts that Democrats are now targeting are in places the president carried by double digits in 2024.

Cook’s U.S. House editor Erin Covey noted in her analysis that tracking spending in key districts gives insight into how both parties view which seats make up the midterm battlefield.

“These races are now seeing heavy outside investment from House Majority PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund and MAGA Inc.’s super PACs, a sign that both sides view these contests as competitive,” Covey wrote.

The editor added that Democrats appear to be competitive in seats that voted for former President Obama but swung to Trump in 2024 — and have not been particularly close in other contests.

articles.title: An attempt to erase race from the Census will harm children
articles.summary: Serving communities with good governance requires knowing what is actually happening on the ground.
articles.body:
Children don’t live in averages. They live in neighborhoods, counties, cities and states, where their experiences and opportunities can differ dramatically.

Serving communities with good governance requires knowing what is actually happening on the ground. That’s true whether you’re a member of Congress deciding how to allocate federal funding, a governor directing resources for struggling school districts or a mayor trying to understand why one neighborhood is thriving while another isn’t.

None of that work is possible without reliable, detailed information. And for more than 200 years , nearly since our nation’s founding and enshrined in the U.S. Constitution, the census has been the backbone of reliable information about who lives in the U.S. It has helped policymakers, community leaders and organizations like ours that are dedicated to child well-being answer two essential questions: How are children and families doing? And where are they facing the greatest challenges?

That information system is now at risk. A newly proposed Census Bureau rule would make several significant changes to how the decennial census counts and describes the nation’s population, with particular implications for children in communities that have historically been harder to count.

Among them, the rule would eliminate questions about race and ethnicity on the decennial census — the one population count Congress requires every 10 years, and an important bedrock for population estimates used in improving accuracy in other federal surveys. Removing these questions from the census would make it much harder to access data on race and ethnicity consistently and accurately over time.

This isn’t the only threat to important information that leaders rely on. The Census Bureau has also delayed the release of data from the American Community Survey , now scheduled for Oct. 29. The American Community Survey annually produces detailed local estimates on income, poverty, education, health insurance and housing costs that the decennial census cannot capture on its own.

Policymakers from governors to school boards all rely on American Community Survey data to draft budgets and develop programs. Foundations like ours rely on it too, using data to guide decisions and understand where children are thriving, where they are struggling and where attention is needed. The Annie E. Casey Foundation’s “ KIDS COUNT Data Book ” relies heavily on American Community Survey estimates to track how children are faring, state by state and across the nation.

National averages that appear to be improving can conceal a very different reality. Child poverty can fall overall while remaining stubbornly high in particular communities. More children can gain health coverage while children in some groups lose it.

For example, the official child poverty rate fell by 2 percentage points between 2019 and 2024 to 15 percent. But the statistic, derived from the American Community Survey, looked very different across states, communities and demographic groups. In West Virginia, 22 percent of children lived in poverty during 2024; in New Hampshire, just 7 percent did.

When those differences are harder to see, the consequences are real. Childcare assistance may not reach communities where families are struggling most with costs, housing investments can miss neighborhoods under the greatest pressure and policymakers can conclude that a program is working even when some children are being left behind.

Scarce public resources are harder to target effectively when leaders cannot clearly and accurately see where needs are greatest or whether investments are effective. Knowing a child’s race or ethnicity does not tell us what that child can achieve or what that family needs but examining outcomes across groups helps reveal whether progress is reaching everyone, and whether policies are working as intended.

Taken together, these two developments point to the same underlying trend: a shrinking ability to see our children and families clearly, at a moment when sound, targeted and effective policymaking depends on it most.

Children are already easy to overlook in our political process. They cannot vote. Many are too young to speak for themselves. They do not choose their neighborhood, their family’s income, their school’s resources or the opportunities within their reach. Adults decide on all of these things.

That gives those who make decisions for children a particular responsibility to understand how they are actually doing, and that means the data behind those decisions deserves protection, not neglect. Today’s children are tomorrow’s employees, customers, employers, voters and community leaders — and their success will shape the strength of our economy and our country.

Members of Congress, state officials, mayors, business leaders and others who depend on Census data should examine the impact these changes will have on the communities they serve — and emphasize the importance of receiving detailed, reliable information on schedule.

Debates about reducing child poverty, improving schools, strengthening families or creating pathways to work all depend on real data and shared facts. That starts with counting and seeing every child fully, reliably, consistently and on time.

Lisa Lawson is president and CEO at the Annie E. Casey Foundation. La June Montgomery Tabron is president and CEO at the W.K. Kellogg Foundation.

articles.title: Hannity takes Zacharia to task over legal credentials
articles.summary: Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on her first briefing with reporters this week and her claiming to be an attorney despite not passing the bar exam. Hannity began his interview of Zacharia on Thursday evening saying, “I know this is a widely viewed interview for you,” in…
articles.body:
Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on her first briefing with reporters this week and her claiming to be an attorney despite not passing the bar exam.

Hannity began his interview of Zacharia on Thursday evening saying, “I know this is a widely viewed interview for you,” in an apparent reference to President Trump, who is a close friend of the Fox host and watches his show regularly.

The host called Zacharia’s first press briefing “widely panned” and noted questions have been raised about her legal credentials and the length of her first briefing, which lasted less than 15 minutes.

“What happened, how did you feel it went personally?” he asked her.

“I was asked to start on Monday, which was Columbus Day, a federal holiday, and was asked to have a press briefing on Tuesday morning,” she said. “What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the briefing with very little prep time. I received briefing materials in the morning Tuesday and went to deliver all of the great results that President Trump is delivering for the American people that is not often spread in the national media.”

Zacharia called the reaction to her first briefing “mixed” and pushed back on complaints she only took questions from conservative media outlets by pointing to the Daily Mail as “not known to be a conservative outlet or friendly to conservatives.”

“Am I hearing that you think the staff should have prepped you better?” Hannity pressed. Zacharia did not answer and instead pointed to her “breaking news” by announcing the administration had asked former Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign in the wake of scandal.

Zacharia has separately faced scrutiny over presenting herself as an attorney despite not passing the bar exam after studying law at Pepperdine University in California.

“You called it a conspiracy theory as it relates to being a lawyer,” Hannity said, referencing another interview Zacharia gave earlier on Thursday. He went on to point out what he said were 15 social media posts “where you identify yourself as an attorney.”

“I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record. … They were retweets of a title that had been given,” she responded.

Hannity asked how Zacharia has spent her first few days as Trump’s top spokesperson.

“Look, that is a very tough room, and I’ve known a lot of press secretaries over the years. Following on the heels of Karoline Leavitt is very tough, and speaking for Donald Trump makes everything tougher,” the Fox host said. “Why not just say, I went to Pepperdine Law School and chose a different career path? Why get into this long, drawn-out definition between the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? Because I don’t think many people see much of a distinction.”

articles.title: Zacharia on China: ‘They don’t even have proper toilets’
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia took a jab at China, saying the country lacked proper toilets, less than a week into the job where she’s already come under fire over her qualifications and performance. “I remember this very distinctly having just come from China, thinking, how is China the next country on the horizon?…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia took a jab at China, saying the country lacked proper toilets, less than a week into the job where she’s already come under fire over her qualifications and performance .

“I remember this very distinctly having just come from China, thinking, how is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets,” Zacharia said during an interview Thursday with Jack Posobiec.

Zacharia, a former spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security who also served as a communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, started her new job as press secretary less than a week ago, filling the position after Karoline Leavitt left the administration earlier this year.

Zacharia held her first press briefing Tuesday morning , where she took three questions from reporters and dropped the news about U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle being asked to resign, following mounting reports of her conduct during her tenure. The briefing lasted about 14 minutes.

The press secretary has made headlines since President Trump announced her appointment. Her job history was brought under question as she previously claimed that she was a lawyer and reports surfaced about her not being licensed to practice law in any state .

The Campaign for Accountability has filed a complaint with the State Bar of California asking for an investigation into her claims of being a lawyer.

When reporters later asked where she passed her bar exam, she responded, “When I moved to China.”

Zacharia moved to China with her husband after graduating for his job at a U.S. private equity firm, and she worked on international transaction law, according to a White House official. Her LinkedIn shows she was an associate on the international practice team for Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013.

articles.title: Carville: Republicans could lose House, Senate despite ‘huge financial advantage’
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville said Thursday that Republicans are “highly likely” to lose House control next month, despite a significant financial advantage and several successful redistricting measures. Carville, in an appearance on NewsNation’s “Cuomo,” doubled down on his analysis giving Democrats the leg up with the midterm elections just more than two weeks away. He…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville said Thursday that Republicans are “highly likely” to lose House control next month, despite a significant financial advantage and several successful redistricting measures .

Carville, in an appearance on NewsNation’s “Cuomo,” doubled down on his analysis giving Democrats the leg up with the midterm elections just more than two weeks away. He added that the GOP could also lose the Senate.

“When this year started, remember, the Republicans had a huge financial advantage. We were all brought up to think money really matters in politics,” the strategist told host Chris Cuomo. “They had a gerrymandered House map, and they had a blood-red Senate map.”

The strategist, who served as former President Clinton’s adviser, noted Democrats needed to focus their efforts on messaging and pushing legislation that is popular with voters.

The Republican Party has led the midterm redistricting battle, with significant pressure from President Trump to get it done. While Democrats followed suit in places like California and Virginia, Republicans were still able to give themselves a potential advantage heading into the 2026 midterms.

With more than $400 million in funding from Trump’s MAGA Inc. and large donations from people like tech mogul Elon Musk, the GOP started the cycle with a leg up. But the president’s low approval ratings and Democrats’ fundraising efforts have made a significant impact on the upcoming election.

“It seems highly likely that they’re going to win the House,” Carville continued Thursday. “I personally … but there’s just a hunch … I think they’ll win the Senate also.”

He added that if Democrats retake the majority in November, they should pass at least five pieces of legislation viewed favorably by most Americans. Some examples he provided include passing a minimum wage hike, reopening rural hospitals and pulling troops out of the Iran war — whether or not Trump would agree to sign the bills into law.

“I think the Democratic agenda is pretty simple,” Carville told NewsNation. “Pass that, which three-quarters of the American people want that they’ll never sign because their interest groups are holding them back.”

Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s partner, currently shows Democrats with a 77 percent chance of retaking control of the House next year. On the Senate side, DDHQ forecasts the left with a narrow lead over Republicans.

articles.title: Trump should try to mediate Turkish-Israeli tensions in the Horn of Africa
articles.summary: Tensions could explode into a new war between any two of the countries that are at loggerheads there, and that could in turn draw in both of those powerful states.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis, as well as America’s ongoing conflict with Iran, have overlapped with, and drawn increasing attention to, simmering rivalries and outright conflicts on the Horn of Africa.

The historian Simon Sebag-Montefiore rightly has asserted that “In this scramble for Africa, the empires are no longer European but Middle Eastern and African.” Indeed, there is no shortage of players in the cauldron that is the Horn. They include Somalia and Somaliland, Ethiopia and Eritrea, Israel and Turkey, as well as Saudi Arabia.

But the Horn hosts extra-regional actors as well. Djibouti, which borders Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia and has coastlines along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, is brimming with foreign facilities. It is host to five extra-regional states — the U.S., China, France, Japan and Italy — all of whom pay hefty fees to station forces there. Camp Lemonnier, the primary U.S. military base in Africa , is home of the Combined Joint Task Force-Horn of Africa headquarters, as well as the Navy Region Europe, Africa, Central infrastructure hub.

China is upgrading what it calls the People’s Liberation Army Support Base. France has maintained a military presence of about 1,500 troops in Djibouti since it granted the country independence in 1971; it is the largest French base in Africa. Japan’s base is its only such facility outside the Japanese mainland. And Italy operates a military support base in the country.

In addition, Turkey maintains its largest overseas base in Somalia, which it has provided with military and economic support since 2011. Israel, the only state to recognize Somaliland, which broke away from Somalia in 1991, officially has no base there, but it has reportedly operated from its territory against the Houthi rebels in Yemen. For its part, the government of Somaliland is seeking Israeli air defense systems to counter what it claims is a buildup of Turkish drones and aircraft in Somalia.

The United Arab Emirates has not formally recognized Somaliland. But like Israel, to which it has close ties, it provides it with military and economic support and has done so since the early 1990s. Most importantly, the Dubai government-owned Dubai Ports World operates the port at Berbera, once a major Soviet naval base until 1977 when Somalia expelled the USSR, and then an American naval base from 1980 to 1990. The Emiratis are currently expanding their air and naval presence at Berbera.

While Djibouti may host the most foreign foreign facilities within its relatively small territory, it is Somaliland that is at the center of one of the Horn’s major rivalries. Last month its president accused Turkey of lobbying states not to recognize its independence. Turkey is a longtime supporter of Somalia; Mogadishu accuses Israel , and to a lesser extent the United Arab Emirates, of promoting Somaliland’s independence.

With Israel and Turkey at loggerheads, especially in Syria — where both countries have a military presence and where Israel has struck a Syrian airbase and drawn Turkish condemnation — the prospects of a clash between the two regional superpowers is very real.

Additionally, the United Arab Emirates openly supports Ethiopia against the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front. At the same time, Addis Ababa accuses neighboring Eritrea of supporting the rebels. Eritrea broke away from Ethiopia in 1993 and went to war with it two years later.

Perhaps not coincidentally, given the Emiratis’ longstanding relationship with Somaliland, and the close ties to Jerusalem of both Ethiopia and Somaliland, landlocked Ethiopia almost reached an agreement with Somaliland for access to the Red Sea. Turkey blocked that agreement. Turkish president Recep Tayyib Erdogan has openly opposed Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. Eritrea now fears that Ethiopia, given its trade and military ties to Israel , and having been foiled in its attempt to access the sea through Somaliland, might attempt to do so through its own territory.

Among its many mediation efforts, the Trump administration has been trying, thus far without success, to create a deconfliction mechanism among Israel, Turkey and Syria. Yet Washington might consider extending its efforts to reduce long-standing Israeli-Turkish tensions on the Horn of Africa, which at any moment could explode into a new war between any two of the countries that are at loggerheads there and that could then draw in both of those powerful states.

Should Israel and Turkey clash in the Horn, their conflict could extend to Syria, destabilize that country and create new opportunities for further Russian intervention or a return of Iranian proxies. That would certainly not be in America’s interest.

Both Israel and Turkey are close American allies. Israel is formally a non-NATO ally, and Turkey is a member of NATO. Washington should make every effort to mitigate, if not reconcile, the two rivals on the Horn of Africa as in Syria, before the current war of words between them explodes into real hostilities in either or both regions.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987 .

articles.title: Peltola, Sullivan spar in fiery final Alaska Senate debate: ‘Let’s have some decorum’
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) sparred Wednesday in a fiery final debate for Senate in Alaska. They tackled the Iran war, economic woes and fisheries in an hourlong debate hosted by Alaska Public Media in partnership with Alaska’s News Source and KTOO. Sullivan, who’s seeking a third term, and Peltola,…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) sparred Wednesday in a fiery final debate for Senate in Alaska.

They tackled the Iran war, economic woes and fisheries in an hourlong debate hosted by Alaska Public Media in partnership with Alaska’s News Source and KTOO. Sullivan, who’s seeking a third term, and Peltola, a former congresswoman who lost Alaska’s at-large House seat in 2024, cast each other as longtime politicians more focused on Washington and the Lower 48 than the issues facing Alaskans at home.

It’s the last scheduled showdown between the rivals as Peltola narrowly leads in recent polls of the race in a state that Trump won by double digits in the last presidential race.

At one point, Sullivan accused Peltola of having gotten the debate’s questions beforehand, arguing that she was reading her answers. The moderators clarified that neither candidate received questions beforehand.

The senator also slammed Peltola for her work with a D.C. lobbying firm after losing her House reelection bid, saying, “You’re walking through the revolving door so much. You must be getting dizzy up here.”

Peltola hit back: “When I lost in ‘24, I went to work in Anchorage on Alaskan issues, municipal issues. Dan’s been in D.C. for 12 years and gotten richer every single one of those years.”

Sullivan rebutted by citing a recent bombshell report from The New York Times , telling voters to “take a look at how she treats Alaskans when the cameras are off” as he accused her of having “abused” staffers.

As Peltola called the claims “unfounded” in crosstalk with Sullivan, a moderator threatened to silence the candidates’ mics, saying, “Let’s have some decorum here.”

Several former Peltola aides who requested anonymity told the Times about profane outbursts and displays of anger throughout the campaign and her former congressional office. The tensions also reportedly led to Peltola a staffing shakeup days before Alaska’s August primary.

Her campaign denied any pattern of problematic behavior, but she acknowledged she “sometimes struggled to deal with her grief” after the 2023 deaths of her mother and husband .

Later in the Thursday night debate, Peltola responded directly to the Times’s reporting.

“I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth,” she said.

“It’s hard not to consider staff members part of your family with the amount of time that you spend together, the kind of pressure that you endure, and I really am very concerned about making sure that we are respectful and respectful of all people,” Peltola said. “I think it’s a real sad statement that I’m such a threat as a candidate that they’re just willing to do and say anything about me to help Dan win.”

Moderators later pressed Sullivan on why he hasn’t denounced derogatory rhetoric from President Trump as strongly as he denounced Peltola’s remarks in the Times reporting.

“Oh, I have denounced the president’s language on these kind of issues,” Sullivan countered, pointing to “ his Megyn Kelly comments and other things like that.”

The rivals found some common ground on protecting youth on online platforms and social media.

“This is an area I’m going to agree with Mary Peltola on. … You can have the greatest economy in the world and job growth, but if your kids are having high levels of depression, young Alaskans, we have to address this,” Sullivan said.

When the candidates were later asked to share a compliment about their competitor, Sullivan said he appreciated that Peltola attended his Marine Corps retirement ceremony. Peltola said she had “three lovely things” to praise the senator on, pointing to his three daughters.

Alaska is considered a solidly red state, but it’s also shown an openness to independents and moderate Democrats. Independent Bill Walker was elected governor in 2014, and Peltola won the Last Frontier’s lone House seat in a 2022 special election before securing a full term. Mark Begich was the last Alaska Democrat to win a Senate race in 2008.

In a potential sign of the race’s high stakes, Trump and Vice President Vance have made recent visits to the state.

Peltola also outraised Sullivan in the second quarter of the year, with nearly $7 million to the incumbent’s $2 million, though Sullivan ended with more cash in the bank.

Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages also put Peltola up by roughly 2 percentage points over Sullivan, with a “likely Democratic” forecast. Cook Political Report, though, still considers the race a “toss up,” with early voting set to start next week.

Alaska is one of just two states that use ranked-choice voting statewide in the general election.

articles.title: Make America protect children again: EPA’s silence betrays the MAHA promise
articles.summary: If the EPA under the current administration will not act to protect children, parents should vote to oust the treacherous perpetrators of widespread poisoning from their positions of power.
articles.body:
More than a year ago, members of Environmental Protection Agency’s Children’s Health Protection Advisory Committee , on which I serve, were asked to help bring the Trump administration’s Make America Healthy Again agenda to fruition.

With a few important caveats, the first MAHA report laid out an argument most of us have been making for years — and who could argue with the desire to protect our children’s health? Despite that agreement, as of this writing, the Trump administration has failed to actualize this bipartisan mission.

The Children’s Health Protection Advisory Committee is the one committee that advises the EPA on how to protect our children from environmental health threats. Under the current administration, however, the committee has not been reconvened since that August 2025 meeting . New members should have been named by March, but those of us who would normally resume work have heard nothing . Previously, the committee successfully provided advice on how to protect children from hazards like take-home pesticide exposures , climate change and plastics . Now, it is utterly silent.

Late last month, more than 70 children’s environmental health leaders, experts and organizations, including former members of the committee, sent a letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin calling on him to fulfill the agency’s statutory obligations and scientific mandate by appointing “ scientifically credible , varied, and balanced expert viewpoints so it is capable of continuing the important mission to protect children’s health.”

In that letter, we argue that the lapse of this important committee is inconsistent with the administration’s MAHA agenda. As MAHA grows unhappier by the day , as promises are broken and ambitions go unfulfilled , a vacant Children’s Health Protection Advisory Committee is yet another example of how this administration is abdicating its responsibility to protect our nation’s kids.

Tragically, it is far too late for my own brilliant, beautiful child. Katherine died a slow, agonizing death at age eight from leukemia. We attribute Katherine’s cancer to unwitting exposure to the toxic pesticide chlorpyrifos. The first move of Trump’s first EPA was to do away with a ban on this chemical .

My beloved daughter’s story is not singular, but it is representative. So many parents have seen their children similarly sicken, and many others worry that what their children eat, drink, breathe or touch will result in ill health or even death. They are right to worry.

The Public Health community seems increasingly receptive to joining together with MAHA on shared concerns . The first MAHA report correctly identifies that 40 percent of American children suffer from a chronic illness, and appropriately lays the blame on toxic products and pollution — along with corporate interference in our political processes.

Like many MAHA moms , I have learned about the failings of our regulatory systems through personal experience. In deciphering links between illness and exposures to chlorpyrifos sprayed for mosquitoes, I unraveled a vast body of peer-reviewed literature linking most of the increase in chronic illnesses to widespread contamination with pesticides, PFAS, plastics and the more than 350,000 synthetic chemicals in production today.

One theme that emerged as I interviewed families and experts for my new book, “ Poisoning Our Children: How Petrochemicals Imperil Every Life on Earth,” is how parents are often shamed and blamed for their children’s illnesses. Yet it is becoming nearly impossible to maintain health given the contaminated and degraded surroundings in which we are all immersed from conception onward. And our regulatory agencies have done precious little to prevent this.

Many believe that the EPA must protect their children from these chemicals, but they do not realize how harmful industries have insidiously dismantled commonsense protections by infiltrating these institutions. Parents across the political spectrum are now seeing this with their own eyes, and they want our political representatives to do something about it. That is their job — to safeguard the nation’s children and support their rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

If we say we love our children, we should not be poisoning them. Most parents, regardless of political affiliation, are concerned about the same thing: threats to their children’s health and future. Most parents love their children deeply and are ready to challenge institutions and change systems to protect them.

If the EPA under the current administration will not act to protect children, parents should vote to oust the treacherous perpetrators of widespread poisoning from their positions of power.

Jean-Marie Kauth , Ph.D., MPH, is a professor at Benedictine University and serves on the Children’s Health Protection Advisory Committee to the Environmental Protection Agency. Her new book, “ Poisoning Our Children ,” is due out from Johns Hopkins University Press in February 2027.

articles.title: Talarico compares campaign to biblical David
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico compared his campaign to biblical figure David, saying he was “going up against our own Goliaths,” ahead of his battleground contest against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in November’s elections. “We are going up against our own Goliaths, those billionaire mega-donors, those corporate PACs, the entire Washington, D.C., establishment,” Talarico said at…
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico compared his campaign to biblical figure David, saying he was “going up against our own Goliaths,” ahead of his battleground contest against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in November’s elections .

“We are going up against our own Goliaths, those billionaire mega-donors, those corporate PACs, the entire Washington, D.C., establishment,” Talarico said at a campaign rally in Texas.

“This race reminds me of that story in the Bible of a shepherd boy who goes up against a giant for 40 days,” Talarico described. “On the day of the fight, he shows up in full armor. He’s carrying so many weapons he has to get someone else to hold his shield.”

“David may not have been as big or as strong as Goliath. He may not have had as many weapons, but he had hope, and he had a slingshot. You are my slingshot,” the Democrat continued, referring to the people of Texas as his “slingshot.”

“And on Nov. 3, those Goliaths aren’t going to know what hit them,” he concluded.

The David and Goliath story from the Bible is generally used to refer to an underdog situation, where a smaller, unlikely challenger faces off against a stronger opponent, according to the Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries .

The comparison comes as Elon Musk — the world’s richest person — poured $158 million into a key super PAC backing Paxton. In the third quarter, Paxton also raised $18 million , adding to what’s already the most expensive Senate race of the cycle.

Talarico and his team, meanwhile, reported $64 million in donations for the third quarter, saying it is the most money ever raised in the third quarter by any Senate candidate.

When Paxton earned President Trump’s endorsement, he was quickly able to defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) but has faced a serious challenge from Talarico despite Texas being a red stronghold.

Talarico has hammered Paxton on his controversial record as the Lone Star State’s top prosecutor who was impeached by the Texas state House in 2023 before being acquitted by the state Senate — and, in audio shared by The New York Times, Paxton contended that his appearance at the GOP’s midterm convention “ dropped our numbers .”

Cook Political Report shifted the race away from Republicans to a “toss-up” rating in August. Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, designated the race as a coin flip but narrowly favoring Democrats, giving Talarico a 54 percent probability of flipping the seat.

articles.title: Collins says she doesn’t regret RFK Jr. vote, tried to block Hegseth
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) does not regret voting for Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s confirmation as secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), reaffirming her position in a Thursday debate. “I agree with him on some issues; I don’t with others,” Collins said. “He was very helpful in expediting the release of the low-income eating assistance…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) does not regret voting for Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s confirmation as secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), reaffirming her position in a Thursday debate.

“I agree with him on some issues; I don’t with others,” Collins said. “He was very helpful in expediting the release of the low-income eating assistance program.”

Collins, locked in a tough reelection battle with former state Sen. Troy Jackson (D), has been criticized by Democrats for not standing up to President Trump when it could affect the outcome of a vote. A New York Times analysis recently found that when Collins votes against the president in his second term, her outcome has prevailed just 15 percent of the time.

While that may not be an issue for most Republican senators running for reelection, it matters in a blue state like Maine, which backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024 and where Collins has staked her reelection bid on standing up to both parties.

Kennedy had a drawn-out confirmation battle to become HHS secretary, driven by his past controversial statements on vaccines and medicine.

Since being confirmed, Kennedy has fired vaccine experts and changed federal guidance on vaccines. Collins spoke out against some of those moves, calling Kennedy’s firing of the entire Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) vaccine panel “excessive.” Collins and Kennedy also clashed over HHS cuts to vaccine funding for HIV/AIDS.

Moderators challenged Collins to name a time when she opposed the president and affected the outcome. Collins mentioned that she rallied senators to oppose Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s confirmation, but that it was unsuccessful in the end.

“There are several examples of that. At one point, I had organized people to vote against Secretary Hegseth,” Collins said. “At the very last minute, at the very last minute, one of our Republicans changed his mind.”

“So that didn’t change the outcome,” the moderator replied.

Jackson used the comment to attack Collins.

“The reality is that 100 percent of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there,” Jackson said.

articles.title: Why the poor vote matters: Under the right threshold, it could be you
articles.summary: Using this broader range reveals a far more vulnerable, unstable terrain.
articles.body:
Late last month, President Trump addressed the latest Census report, Poverty in the United States: 2025 , saying, “We have the best poverty numbers ever in the history of the country,” and “there is less poverty now than in any time in the history of the country.”

This is only true if we take the most limited data from the report and ignore the harsh reality facing the nation.

The president was referring to the 10.2 percent poverty rate as measured by the official poverty measure. This is, however, the wrong data to be looking at. Instead, we should focus on the supplemental poverty measure data.

While the official poverty measure is based solely on pre-tax household income, the supplemental poverty measure accounts for taxes, non-cash benefits, necessary out of pocket expenses and geographic variations in housing costs. Developed by the National Academy of Sciences, it is widely recognized by economists, social scientists and government agencies as a more accurate measure of economic hardship.

According to the supplemental poverty measure, 13.1 percent — or approximately 44 million people — were poor in 2025.

Although a better gauge, the supplemental poverty measure is still constrained by a notoriously low threshold. The Center for Poverty and Social Policy at Columbia University shared estimates with the Kairos Center, where I work, based on data from the 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplement to the Current Population Survey.

The estimates show that, depending on location and whether they rent or have a mortgage, an individual’s income must be between approximately $15,500 and $28,000 to meet the threshold. Similarly, the income for a two-adult, two-child household must be between about $33,000 and $61,000.

In other words, these numbers are still too small to capture the real economic hardship households are facing, especially amid rising costs of living, defunded social welfare programs, the 2025 tariffs, war on Iran and other harmful policies. With heating costs on the rise, many are anticipating a “heat or eat” winter coming soon.

Another compounding factor is H.R. 1 , the “One, Big Beautiful Bill Act” which went into effect last year. It made the largest cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — the country’s most extensive food security program — in its entire history. Since then, 5.5 million people have lost their SNAP benefits, including over 1 million children. The effects of these cuts travel through the food supply chain , from growers to grocers, retailers, community-based networks, churches, SNAP recipients and their families, while food pantries face shortages nationwide.

What’s happening to SNAP will soon happen to healthcare. In September, 750,000 people lost their Affordable Care Act coverage. Additionally, America awaits more of the devastating $1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid , which currently provides healthcare to 80 million people and accounts for one-fifth of all hospital care spending . As Medicaid loses hundreds of billions of dollars, millions of people will lose coverage, and millions more will be affected by job losses, reduced services and hospital closures .

To estimate the impact of these conditions, the Kairos Center and the Center on Poverty and Social Policy at Columbia University worked to identify the population living at or below 250 percent of the poverty threshold. Depending on where someone lives, this would include individuals earning up to approximately $71,000 or a family of four with household incomes of up to $153,000.

Using this broader range reveals a far more vulnerable, unstable terrain: 53 percent of the population — or 180 million people — are poor, low-income or economically fragile, living within one or two emergencies of economic ruin. The first emergency might push a family into unsustainable debt burdens, while the second means losing their electricity, heat, water or home.

These 180 million people are disproportionately people of color: 71.8 percent of the Latino/Hispanic population (50.3 million), 69.3 percent of the Black, non-Latino population (27.3 million), 48.5 percent of the Asian American-Pacific Islander population (12.3 million) and 56.6 percent (8.1 million) of a multi-racial, non-Latino population. The white non-Latino population has the lowest rates at 43.4 percent but the greatest number of people, 82 million, experiencing economic fragility. This threshold also includes more than 60 percent of our children (44 million) and the majority of our elders (34 million).

Notably, this crisis isn’t just affecting one region of the country but unfolding from coast to coast and everywhere in between.

These conditions help explain why affordability has become the defining issue of the midterm elections — and why this massive population of 180 million people, including at least 135 million adults and tens of millions of eligible voters, matters in November.

This low-income electorate has often accounted for one-third of the eligible voting population. Although these 80-90 million people represent a massive, potentially tide-shifting segment of voters, their turnout rate is often 20 percentage points lower than higher-income voters. Structural barriers, voter suppression and intimidation contribute to these turnout disparities, along with the general belief that their priorities are not politically relevant.

This year, the needs of these 180 million poor, low-income and economically fragile households are a majority issue. These voters are hungry, uninsured, watching fuel costs rise and fearing eviction, wondering which bills can wait until next month. They are tired of being over-policed, in debt and under-employed. They are ready for a change.

Shailly Gupta Barnes is the director of policy and research at the Kairos Center and was the founding policy director of the Poor People’s Campaign .

articles.title: Americans back Trump's decision against livestreaming Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution
articles.summary: Trump canceled the Nidal Hasan firing squad execution livestream, but victims' families will still be able to witness the Fort Hood shooter's scheduled death.
articles.body: Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital were overwhelmingly pleased with President Donald Trump's decision to call off livestreaming the Fort Hood shooter’s planned firing squad execution after the Pentagon had announced it would be livestreamed for public viewing. "I'm really glad that he called it off, because I feel like it's not really a deterrent, it's more like a shock effect," Sylvia from Arizona told Fox News Digital. "I don't think we really need that in this country right now." "The only other countries that really do that are like North Korea," David from Arizona said. "We don't want to be North Korea." AMERICANS DRAW THE LINE AT LIVESTREAMING ‘SPECTACLE’ OF FORT HOOD SHOOTER'S EXECUTION: ‘IT’S AN ABOMINATION’ "I never approved of the idea of it being public in the first place," Nate from Virginia said. "I think it's just ridiculous to make a spectacle out of an execution, especially in 2026 of all time." War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Nidal Hasan’s execution, set for Dec. 3, would be publicly available via livestream. Trump took to Truth Social on Thursday to announce that while livestreaming the execution could serve as a deterrent to terrorism, the execution would not be available for public viewing as he acknowledged that many Americans would rather not witness Hasan's death. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. FORT HOOD SURVIVORS PRAISE TRUMP FOR SCRAPPING HASAN EXECUTION LIVESTREAM: ‘WE’RE NOT BARBARIC’ Despite the execution not being publicly available, Trump confirmed that the family members of the victims who died in the 2009 shooting "deserve to witness JUSTICE" and will be permitted to attend in person. "Well, maybe he has a conscience now," one person said about Trump’s reversal of the Pentagon’s decision to livestream the execution. Some Americans who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that Trump’s decision to call off the livestreaming was to save face after criticism of the proposal was circulating, with many arguing that livestreaming the execution would turn it into a spectacle and could easily be exposed to children. "I think it was trying to save his image," Ivy from Georgia said. "He doesn't wanna look like a bad person, but at the end of the day, we all know who he really is — a piece of s---," Ivy said. "I think it was just so clearly an unpopular thing to do that he realized it would probably do more harm to his public image than good," Nate said. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shooting, killed 13 and injured 32 people when he shouted "Allahu Akbar" and opened fire at a military base in Texas. The mass killer is now 56 years old and uses a wheelchair after he was left partially paralyzed from being shot by police officers during his arrest almost 17 years ago. TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE Only one person who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that livestreaming the execution would have been a good idea, even adding that he would have watched the livestream himself. "Yeah, I would watch," Daniel from Virginia said. "Because I wouldn't want somebody to kill another person, you know what I mean? That person should be held wrong for what he's done." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hasan was sentenced to death during his 2013 military trial after being found guilty on all 42 counts. His execution is set to be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades.

articles.title: ICE officers ‘did not identify themselves’ ahead of Bronx shooting: Lawyers
articles.summary: Lawyers for the man shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New York City say the officers involved “did not identify themselves” before they opened fire on him, according to recent court filings. On Oct. 8, Oscar Belgal was picking up his 5-year-old son before he was stopped by ICE officers who did not…
articles.body:
Lawyers for the man shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New York City say the officers involved “did not identify themselves” before they opened fire on him, according to recent court filings.

On Oct. 8, Oscar Belgal was picking up his 5-year-old son before he was stopped by ICE officers who did not “show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Legal Aid Society, a group representing Belgal, described.

The group continued in the 58-page document filed Wednesday that “without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat.”

“One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed. Believing that his dad had been fatally shot, his son screamed hysterically that the masked men had killed his father,” the filing states.

The incident, which was captured on ICE officer body cameras, resulted in Belgal being taken to an area hospital, while his child remains unharmed and with a family member, according to New York Police Department (NYPD) Commissioner Jessica Tisch. The body camera footage has not been released.

Legal Aid attorneys serving as counsel for Belgal, Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, said in a press release that their client’s ICE detention was “unlawful from its inception.”

“With a bullet still lodged in his neck and his serious medical needs unmet, every additional day in custody puts him at further risk. The Court must intervene and order his immediate release,” McAninch and Williams stated.

In the hours following the shooting , New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said he called President Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to negotiate Belgal’s release from federal custody but was “unsuccessful.”

Mullin detailed the phone call , saying at a press conference that Trump agreed to move Belgal to the NYPD’s custody if charges against him were to be prosecuted, but Mamdani did not agree, according to Mullin.

The secretary further accused Belgal of participating in “extensive criminal activity” and stated ICE officers involved in the incident were not aware of Belgal’s son in the backseat. Mullin stated the ICE officers will be put on administrative leave while the department investigates the incident.

Mamdani has also called for ICE to release the body-camera footage of the incident. The NYPD has already released body-camera footage from its officers of the moments after the shooting.

When asked about the filing, DHS referred The Hill to Mullin’s Friday press conference where he stated, “during a targeted fugitive operation on September 18, ICE attempted to arrest Belgal in the Bronx.”

“He disobeyed ICE officers’ lawful commands and fled law enforcement. For the safety of the general public, ICE stood down and did not pursue him that day,” Mullin continued.

articles.title: Zacharia says Trump didn’t ask whether she passed bar exam
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia weighed in on the controversy surrounding her law career Friday, saying President Trump did not ask questions about whether she passed the bar exam when she was appointed to her role. When asked by Fox News about reporting that she did not pass the test, Zacharia said, “Those questions…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia weighed in on the controversy surrounding her law career Friday, saying President Trump did not ask questions about whether she passed the bar exam when she was appointed to her role.

When asked by Fox News about reporting that she did not pass the test, Zacharia said, “Those questions weren’t asked.”

“I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel,” she told the “ Fox & Friends ” hosts. “The reason that I was hired was to represent the president in the press.”

Zacharia started making headlines as soon as she stepped in to her new role, particularly about her claims of being a lawyer as reports surfaced about her not being licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. A watchdog group called the Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California asking for an investigation into her claim.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the group’s executive director, said in a statement.

Reporters also pressed her on where she passed the exam.

The press secretary responded, “When I moved to China.”

Zacharia later said she misheard the question .

“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” she told The New York Times on Wednesday. The president also called her “an attorney” in his Truth Social post announcing her appointment as his spokesperson.

The Wall Street Journal also reported that Zacharia took the California bar exam after she received her law degree from Pepperdine University, but she did not pass . She said Thursday that the results of the test are “ somewhat inconsequential .”

Zacharia was previously a communications adviser for Trump Media and Technology Group, the company behind the president’s Truth Social platform, and also served at one time as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.

She started her new role earlier this week, holding a 14-minute press briefing Tuesday morning . During the brief exchange with reporters, she took three questions and dropped the news about the resignation of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.

Zacharia was appointed to fill the gap left by Karoline Leavitt, who departed the administration earlier this year.

articles.title: Are dark days ahead for Republicans after the midterm elections?
articles.summary: President Donald Trump faces potential backlash from Republican voters during the midterms, which could lead to increased Congressional scrutiny from Democrats if they win control of the House and Senate.
articles.body:
You have to hand it to President Trump. He has managed to offend Democrats, alienate independents, and now, just for good measure, turn off Republicans, too.

This is not exactly a brilliant political strategy with the midterm elections just a few weeks away.

Apparently, even some Republicans have had enough. They’re tired of the chaos, tired of the constant feuding, tired of the daily drama. In a word — make that two words — they’re tired of Donald Trump.

The Times quotes a former Republican member of the Michigan House of Representatives who put it this way: “People are tired. The whole divider-in-chief thing, it’s gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.”

And it’s a safe bet that he’s not alone.

So what is Trump’s solution? He is telling Republicans to vote as if he were on the ballot. Careful what you wish for. Some Republicans may take his advice — and stay home.

That’s not exactly what Trump had in mind, but then again, nobody has ever accused him of underestimating his own popularity. Trump has always been his own biggest fan. You get the impression that he thinks that because he’s in love with himself, everybody else should be too.

We’ll know soon enough whether he can persuade disillusioned Republicans to show up on Election Day. His pitch is simple: Vote Republican or you’ll regret it. Because if Democrats take control of Congress, he warns, dark days are ahead.

Maybe. But here’s something we can say with considerably more confidence: If Democrats take the House — and possibly the Senate — dark days really will be ahead. This is especially so for Trump and for Republicans, who will suddenly discover what life is like when the other team gets to call the plays.

So what can the president expect if his party winds up on the outside looking in? Let’s start with impeachment. The smarter Democrats may recognize that impeaching Trump for a third time would be a political mistake. Even Americans who can’t stand Trump may have little appetite for another impeachment circus.

But the hard left won’t be interested in political wisdom. They will want to publicly humiliate Trump at any cost. And there’s a decent chance that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), if he becomes speaker, will go wobbly. He will discover that standing up to his party’s loudest voices is harder than giving in to them.

As for high crimes and misdemeanors, Democrats will undoubtedly find something that fits their definition. Take your pick: deportations, presidential pardons, the demolition of the White House East Wing, the war in Iran.

And why stop with Trump himself? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and assorted other Trump loyalists could find themselves in the congressional crosshairs.

Then come the investigations. Lots and lots of investigations.

The Trump family business. Jeffrey Epstein. Tariffs. The White House ballroom. The president’s attacks on his critics in the news media. Taxpayer-funded advertisements that just happen to make Trump look wonderful.

Democrats may even try to subpoena the president himself. Good luck with that. He’ll tell them what they can do with their subpoena before he even thinks about going to Capitol Hill to answer questions thrown at him by Democrats who loathe everything about him.

But they might have better luck dragging people around him before congressional committees, people like his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, who knows the kind of stuff Democrats would love to hear from her — while she’s under oath. Another long shot, bordering on no way she would talk. But Democrats won’t care — anything to make Team Trump miserable.

So, get ready for hearings, subpoenas, accusations, counteraccusations and enough political theater to keep cable news in business for another decade.

Of course, none of this is inevitable. Polls have been wrong before. They could be wrong again. But I wouldn’t bet on it.

Too many polls are telling us the same thing: Trump is about as popular — maybe even a little less popular — than the flu. And since midterm elections are essentially a report card on the president, Republicans have good reason to worry —especially when the president is determined to make the election all about himself.

And if the results are as bad as Republicans fear, we won’t have to wait long for the postmortem. It’ll probably begin about 10 seconds after the polls close.

Trump will blame the fake news media. He’ll blame rigged elections. He’ll blame RINOs, disloyal Republicans, lousy candidates and anybody else who happens to be within shouting distance.

But there’s one thing we can count on: Whatever happens on Election Day, Trump will find somebody to blame. And we all know who it won’t be.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page .

It’s Friday. Just more than two weeks until we change the clocks back to standard time. Anyone else ready for that “extra hour” of sleep? 😴

Hegseth’s execution livestream plan scrapped

Republicans face mounting midterm pressure

Programming note : Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

That’s the question swirling around the White House as the preemptive blame game begins for what could be a tough Election Day for Republicans.

Among those angling for the chief of staff position if Susie Wiles departs: deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller , home finance chief (and briefly director of national intelligence) Bill Pulte and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin , according to The Washington Post .

Also in the mix is Jay Clayton , who was just moved from U.S. attorney to director of national intelligence, Politico Playbook reported this morning . That followed Playbook’s reporting on Thursday that broke the seal on the Wiles drama, with sources saying President Trump was making calls about potential replacements.

The White House says it’s all fake news.

“Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Thursday.

Anthony Scaramucci lasted 11 days as Trump’s communications director during his first term.

It’s now been seven days since the president announced that Katie Zacharia would replace Karoline Leavitt — and it’s not going well.

Zacharia faced tough questions on Fox News last night and again this morning as she seeks to clear up confusion around her legal credentials.

She admitted to Sean Hannity last night that she did not pass the bar exam. And in an interview with “Fox & Friends” this morning, she said the issue didn’t come up in her conversations with Trump about the job.

Zacharia also went to the “sticks” today outside the White House, where Trump officials typically take questions from reporters.

“I’m not taking any questions, but I want to let you know that I’m looking forward to working with all of you so much,” she told reporters. “Please get my number, reach out to me, call me, text me, email me.”

Another question a lot of people around here are asking today: Who decided to throttle Ukraine’s access to Elon Musk ’s satellite network earlier this week?

Musk said it wasn’t him , pointing the finger at the Trump administration. But still no word on where exactly the order came from.

Reuters reported last night that it came from inside the White House, and that the Pentagon “received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.”

A U.S. official told NewsNation this morning: “No such request was ever made by the President.”

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton is all over the Republican reaction to the Starshield drama.

Four Republican senators signed a bipartisan letter to the Pentagon’s inspector general, demanding he investigate whether any U.S. government officials “directed” or “authorized” changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements or Starlink services affecting Ukraine.

Among the four were two members of the Senate Intelligence Committee, Sens. Susan Collins (Maine) and John Cornyn (Texas), along with Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Thom Tillis (N.C.).

John Ullyot , a former spokesperson for the Senate Armed Services Committee and former deputy assistant to Trump, said senators have good reason to suspect the Pentagon’s involvement in the decision.

“Hegseth reportedly cut off weapons to Ukraine without the President’s sign-off three times in his first six months on the job, so it’s not surprising senators want to know if he was involved here as well,” Ullyot said.

Trump’s decision to scrap Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ‘s plan to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan followed days of bipartisan backlash , public opposition and questions from within his own administration.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle pushed back on the original proposal, with some Republicans warning that the footage could become a recruiting tool for terrorists.

Even Vice President Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) made clear they had no interest in watching.

The public wasn’t exactly enthusiastic, either. A recent YouGov poll found 71 percent of Americans opposed livestreaming executions, including a majority of GOP respondents.

Trump himself had been noncommittal about the plan before pulling the plug Thursday.

Hasan’s execution is still scheduled for Dec. 3, with only immediate family members of the victims allowed to attend.

And Hegseth? : The Pentagon says he and Trump are “ completely aligned ” on the decision.

Trump is headed to Georgia today, hoping to give Republicans a much-needed boost as the clock ticks down to the midterm elections.

With just more than two weeks to go, the president is trying to help Rep. Mike Collins (R) unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) in a race that could help determine control of the Senate next year.

The final push: The Peach State is the latest stop in Trump’s campaign blitz , which has taken him to Ohio, Arizona and Montana in recent days.

And the president is keeping his foot on the gas, with Kentucky next on his schedule Saturday. Vance has also been hitting the trail, including a stop in Michigan on Thursday.

Meanwhile, in other races: Trump is doubling down on his endorsement of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton after taking shots at Cornyn, keeping the spotlight on a messy GOP fight. In an interview Thursday, he told Newsmax that he has no regrets about his decision to back Paxton in the Texas Senate race.

“I think Cornyn would have lost,” he said. “Here’s the way I look at it: Ken Paxton, some people don’t love him, but everybody admits he was the best attorney general in the history of Texas, one of the best in the country.”

His remarks also come as polls show Paxton’s Democratic challenger James Talarico with a slight lead .

The Cook Political Report shifted 11 more House races toward Democrats on Friday, including GOP-held districts in Minnesota and Ohio.

The move shows just how much ground Republicans need to defend to stay in power — and how little time they have left.
